title: The Big 5
article_body:
## What Buyers Actually Research

Think about the last time you made a significant purchase. Maybe it was a service for your business, a piece of equipment, or a major home improvement. Before you reached out to anyone, you researched. You looked up pricing. You read about potential problems. You compared your options. You checked reviews. You searched for the best in the category.

Every serious buyer does the same thing. The topics they research are consistent across industries, price points, and buyer types. They are called The Big 5, and they represent the five content categories that have the greatest impact on trust and purchasing decisions.

## The Five Topics

The first topic is cost and price. The first question in almost every buyer's mind is what something will cost. When a company does not address this question openly, buyers feel frustrated and suspicious. They leave. The companies that address pricing honestly, including what drives cost up and down and why some providers charge more, consistently earn more trust than those that withhold this information.

The second topic is problems and concerns. Buyers worry about what can go wrong. They search for the downsides, the complaints, the situations where a product or service is not a good fit. A company willing to address these concerns honestly, to say out loud that their solution is not right for everyone, builds more trust than one that only promotes its strengths. This principle is called the Law of the Coin: every purchase has two sides, and buyers will find both.

The third topic is comparisons and alternatives. Buyers compare. It is how they make confident decisions. They stack options against each other. They want to know how your product differs from the competition, when another option might be better, and how to evaluate the difference. The companies that lead this conversation, rather than pretending competitors do not exist, are seen as far more credible.

The fourth topic is reviews. Buyers want to know what real customers experienced. They read the negative reviews first. They want to understand what went wrong, how the company handled it, and whether the problems matter for their specific situation. Companies that actively generate reviews, create their own honest product review content, and respond openly to feedback build trust far faster than those that ignore this topic.

The fifth topic is best-in-class options. Buyers search for the best, the top, the most reliable, the highest-rated. They use phrases like best, most, top, and safest as they narrow down their choices. Companies that create content around these searches, including honest lists of the best options in their category or market, capture buyers at the moment they are closest to a decision.

## Why Most Companies Avoid These Topics

Most businesses know these are the topics buyers care about most. Most still refuse to address them. The reasons are predictable: they worry about scaring buyers with pricing, about empowering competitors, about appearing biased when discussing comparisons. These fears are understandable but wrong.

Buyers are going to find this information somewhere. They will search until they get it. The company that provides it earns the relationship. The company that withholds it sends the buyer to whoever is willing to be transparent. Choosing not to address Big 5 topics is not neutrality. It is a decision to let someone else have the conversation.

## The Big 5 and AI Visibility

As AI search tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI Overviews become more influential in how buyers discover and evaluate options, Big 5 content has become even more important. AI systems draw heavily on honest, thorough, expert content when making recommendations. The same characteristics that make Big 5 content rank well in traditional search, depth, transparency, and genuine expertise, are the same characteristics that make AI more likely to recommend your business.

## Getting Started

Start with your core product or service and work through each of the five topics in order. Begin with cost and price because it has the most immediate sales impact. Use your sales team as a resource. Ask them what questions they answer on every call. Every one of those questions is a piece of Big 5 content waiting to be written. Commit to three new pieces per week and build from there.
excerpt: Every buyer researches the same five subjects before making a significant purchase. Most companies refuse to address them. That refusal is costing them business every day. The Big 5 gives you a content framework built around how buyers actually behave.
what_youll_learn: The Big 5 represent the questions every buyer asks before making a significant purchase. Most companies avoid these topics, which is exactly why addressing them builds so much trust.
Cost and price content is the most powerful place to start. Buyers who cannot find pricing leave your website and find a competitor who will tell them.

Problems content builds trust by showing both sides of a purchase decision, a practice the book calls the Law of the Coin. Addressing what can go wrong before the buyer asks signals radical transparency.
Comparison content is not a risk. Buyers are going to compare their options regardless. The companies willing to lead that conversation on their own website win.
Reviews and best-in-class content round out the Big 5, and both have become more important as AI systems draw on exactly this type of content to make purchasing recommendations.
The Big 5 applies to every content format, not just blog articles. Video, podcasts, social posts, and YouTube all benefit from the same five-topic framework.

key_questions.question: What are The Big 5 content topics?
key_questions.answer: The Big 5 are: cost and price, problems and concerns, comparisons and alternatives, reviews, and best-in-class options. These are the five subjects every buyer researches before making a significant purchase, regardless of industry.

key_questions.question: Why do most companies avoid The Big 5?
key_questions.answer: Most companies avoid these topics out of fear. They worry that publishing pricing will scare buyers away, that acknowledging problems will undermine confidence in their product, or that running honest comparisons will send buyers to competitors. The opposite is true. Buyers are going to research these topics no matter what. The companies that address them earn trust. The ones that stay silent lose it.

key_questions.question: Which of The Big 5 should I start with?
key_questions.answer: Start with cost and price content. It is the topic buyers are most desperate for and the one most companies refuse to address. A well-written pricing article or video typically has the most immediate impact on the sales process. Once that is in place, move to problems content, then comparisons, reviews, and best-in-class content for your core products and services.

key_questions.question: Does The Big 5 apply to video as well as written content?
key_questions.answer: Yes. The Big 5 originated as a written content framework but applies equally to video, podcasts, and social media. In fact, some of the most successful Big 5 implementations involve YouTube videos, short-form social clips, and podcast episodes built around the same five topics.

key_questions.question: How often should I be publishing Big 5 content?
key_questions.answer: A minimum of three new pieces of Big 5 content per week. That pace, sustained over time, builds the content library needed to rank in search, get recommended by AI, and give your sales team assets to use throughout the buyer's journey.

title: Cost and Price Content
article_body:
When someone visits your website and wants to know what you charge, one of two things happens. They find the information and feel relieved. Or they don't find it and leave — often within seconds. Most companies assume buyers will call if they can't find pricing. They don't. They search until they find a company willing to answer the question, and that's the company that gets the call.

Marcus Sheridan calls the feeling a buyer gets when they can't find pricing the "F-word of the internet" — frustration. And the frustration doesn't come from the absence of an exact number. It comes from the sense that the company knows the answer and is deliberately withholding it. The moment a buyer suspects information is being hidden, trust erodes. That trust is very hard to rebuild once it's gone.

## Why Most Businesses Don't Publish Pricing

When you talk to businesses about why they don't address cost online, the explanations tend to follow the same three patterns.

The first is complexity. "Every job is different. It depends." This is true, but buyers know prices vary. They're not asking for a binding quote. They're asking for a range, an explanation of what affects the number, and a general sense of what to expect. A thoughtful answer that covers the variables is exactly what they want.

The second is competitive exposure. "If we publish our prices, competitors will find out." Ask any experienced salesperson on your team whether they have a sense of what competitors charge. Of course they do. Pricing is rarely a secret inside an industry. The real risk isn't that a competitor learns your pricing — it's that your competitor educates your buyers before you do.

The third is buyer avoidance. "Talking about price will scare people off." What actually scares buyers is the opposite: not being able to find information. Ignorance breeds doubt. Doubt leads to inaction. And inaction means the lead never converts. Transparency relieves anxiety, and relieved buyers are far more likely to take the next step.

## The $35 Million Article

In 2009, during a recession, Marcus Sheridan's pool company River Pools was struggling. In a moment of desperation, he decided to write an article explaining the full cost of a fiberglass swimming pool — becoming the first pool company in the world to address pricing on their website. He explained what drives cost up, what drives it down, what different options and packages typically cost, why some pool companies charge more than others, and where River Pools generally fell.

He never published an exact price. He educated buyers about the full landscape of what a pool costs and why.

The result: that one article has now generated millions of views, thousands of sales appointments, and more than $35 million in revenue. It took 45 minutes to write. Prospects began calling in and thanking the company just for being willing to talk about pricing openly. Trust was established before the first conversation even started.

## The Perfect Pricing Page

IMPACT has helped hundreds of companies build what they call the Perfect Pricing Page. The format is designed to give buyers everything they need to understand cost without requiring you to publish a fixed price list. The most important elements to address are:

What drives cost up in your industry? Buyers want to understand what they're paying for. Explain the factors — quality of materials, scope of work, specialized expertise, longer timelines — that push the price higher.

What drives cost down? Are there ways to get a more affordable version? What do buyers sacrifice in exchange for a lower price? This transparency helps buyers make an informed choice rather than choosing cheapest by default because no one educated them otherwise.

Why are some companies more expensive? Explain the reasons — premium materials, more experienced teams, stronger warranties, additional services. Help buyers understand what they're actually getting for a higher price.

Why are some companies cheaper? This is a question buyers are asking regardless. If competitors undercut you, explain what that lower price usually means in practice — offshore production, thinner margins, less experienced personnel, minimal service after the sale.

Where does your pricing generally fall? Be clear about where you sit in the market and why. Did you make a deliberate choice about quality? Explain it. Help buyers understand what they're getting for the price and why you're positioned where you are.

Beyond those five, the Perfect Pricing Page format can also include common pricing tiers (low-end, mid-tier, high-end), financing options, lifetime cost versus initial cost, visual examples with corresponding price ranges, and a pricing-related FAQ section.

## How This Works Across Formats

Cost and price content works in written articles, videos, podcasts, and social media. The format is the same regardless of medium: educate buyers about the full landscape of pricing in your industry, explain what they should expect to pay and why, and give them the context they need to evaluate options intelligently. Whether someone reads a blog post or watches a video, the effect is the same — they arrive at a conversation with you already informed, already trusting, and far more ready to move forward.

The companies that address pricing openly consistently report stronger inbound leads, shorter sales cycles, and higher close rates. Buyers who already understand cost don't need to be sold — they've already evaluated options and chosen you based on transparency alone.
excerpt: Buyers want to know what things cost before they reach out. Publishing honest pricing content is one of the highest-trust moves a business can make — and one of the most powerful lead generators available.
what_youll_learn: Most buyers leave a website within 10 seconds if they can't find pricing information — and they don't call to ask. They just move on.
You don't need to publish an exact price. You need to explain what drives cost up, what drives it down, and where your pricing generally falls.
The three most common objections to publishing pricing — complex variables, competitive exposure, and scaring buyers away — don't hold up under scrutiny.
Pricing transparency builds trust because when a buyer can't find pricing, they assume you're hiding something.
One article about fiberglass pool costs generated more than $35 million in revenue for River Pools — without ever stating an exact price.
The Perfect Pricing Page format gives you a repeatable structure for addressing pricing honestly on your website.

key_questions.question: What if our pricing is complex and varies by job?
key_questions.answer: Buyers already expect prices to vary. What they want is a range, an explanation of what drives cost up and down, and a sense of what to expect. You can address the question thoroughly without committing to an exact number.

key_questions.question: Won't publishing pricing let competitors know what we charge?
key_questions.answer: Your experienced salespeople already have a good sense of what competitors charge, and vice versa. Pricing is rarely a secret inside an industry. The bigger risk is letting competitors educate your buyers before you do.

key_questions.question: Will transparent pricing scare buyers away?
key_questions.answer: The opposite tends to happen. Buyers feel frustrated when they can't find pricing, not when they find it. Transparency builds trust. Hiding information breeds doubt.

key_questions.question: What is the Perfect Pricing Page?
key_questions.answer: It's a format for covering pricing thoroughly: what drives costs up, what drives them down, why some companies charge more, why some charge less, where your pricing generally falls, common tiers or packages, and pricing-related FAQs.

key_questions.question: Does this work for service businesses, not just product companies?
key_questions.answer: Yes. Service businesses often have the most to gain from pricing transparency because their markets tend to have almost no pricing information available online, making any company willing to address it stand out immediately.

title: Problems Content
article_body:
Buyers are more worried about what could go wrong than excited about what could go right. This isn't cynicism — it's how purchasing decisions are made. When someone is considering a significant buy, they think about the risks. They hunt for horror stories. They search for reasons not to buy something, because they know that the one-star reviews are where the truth lives.

Think about your own behavior on Amazon. When you're seriously evaluating something, do you scroll through the five-star reviews first? Probably not. You go straight to the complaints, the disappointments, the warnings. You're trying to figure out whether this purchase could be a mistake.

Your potential customers are doing the same thing with your product or service. And if you don't provide that honest picture, they'll find it somewhere else — often from a source with less context and less goodwill toward your brand.

## The Law of the Coin

Every purchase has two sides, like a coin. There are reasons to buy and reasons not to buy. The Law of the Coin says businesses should show both. Most companies only show one side — the positive case for their product. They leave buyers to discover the other side on their own, usually from competitors, review sites, or disgruntled customers.

When you address problems proactively, you do two things. First, you give buyers the honest information they're going to find anyway — just from you, in context, with nuance. Second, you disarm them. A buyer who expected you to hide the downsides and instead finds you laying them out openly experiences something unexpected: trust. You've shown that you care more about their making a good decision than about making a sale.

That shift in the buyer's perception is enormously powerful. Once a buyer feels like you're on their side rather than trying to sell them something, they're much more likely to move forward.

## What Problems Content Looks Like in Practice

Sheffield Metals, a metal roofing manufacturer based in the Midwest, is one of the clearest examples of this principle applied well. They published an article called "Metal Roofing Problems: 7 Common Issues That Could Affect Your Roof." The opening line sets the tone immediately: "No product in the world is perfect, no matter how much money it's worth or how well it's cared for."

The article covers the seven most common problems that can occur with a metal roof, explains how to avoid each one, and is honest about the fact that a metal roof is not right for everyone — even though metal roofing is the only type of roof they sell. That last point is remarkable. Sheffield Metals is openly telling potential customers that their product might not be the right choice.

The result: more than one million views on the article, more than half a million views on the companion YouTube video, and a massive increase in brand recognition and sales across North America. Sheffield Metals is now one of the most trusted metal roofing brands in the country, and problems content is a significant part of how that happened.

## How to Find the Right Problems to Address

The starting point is your sales team. Every objection they hear regularly in the sales process is a problem worth addressing in content. The questions that start with "Is it true that..." or "I heard there were issues with..." or "I'm worried about..." — these are your content topics.

Add to that your one-star reviews, customer support tickets, and post-sale complaints. These are the exact concerns buyers are researching before they reach out. If you're seeing a pattern, buyers are searching for it.

The goal isn't to create doubt. It's to address doubts that already exist, before a buyer finds a less charitable version of the answer somewhere else. The greatest way to resolve a concern is to address it before it becomes a concern.

## Problems Content Works Across Formats

This category of content performs well in written articles, videos, and podcast discussions. A video titled "7 Problems with [Product Type] and How to Avoid Them" follows the same logic as a written article — it gives buyers honest information in a format that builds personal connection and trust.

The businesses that embrace problems content consistently report that it attracts more qualified leads, not fewer. Because buyers who make it through an honest assessment of the downsides and still want to talk to you are genuinely interested. They're not going to waste your time, and you're not going to waste theirs.
excerpt: Buyers research what could go wrong before they commit. Addressing the drawbacks, risks, and concerns around your product or service builds more trust than any marketing claim you could make.
what_youll_learn: Buyers research negatives more actively than positives. When they read reviews, they go straight to the one-star entries.
Every product and service has two sides: reasons to buy and reasons not to buy. The Law of the Coin says you should show both.
Proactively addressing problems disarms potential customers and builds trust faster than almost any other content approach.
Sheffield Metals addressed the seven most common problems with metal roofing. That article generated more than one million views.
The best way to resolve a concern is to address it before it becomes a concern.
Problems content requires courage, but the businesses that embrace it consistently outperform those that avoid it.

key_questions.question: Won't talking about our product's problems scare people off?
key_questions.answer: The opposite tends to happen. Buyers are already researching your product's problems whether you address them or not. When you address them openly, buyers trust you more because you're not hiding anything. The ones who stay after reading your honest assessment are far more qualified leads.

key_questions.question: What kinds of problems should we address?
key_questions.answer: Start with the doubts, fears, objections, and concerns your sales team hears most often. Common patterns include: 'Is it true that...' questions, competitor claims, known industry drawbacks, situations where your product is not the best fit, and past incidents or issues that buyers reference.

key_questions.question: Should we say our product isn't right for everyone?
key_questions.answer: Yes, when it's true. Sheffield Metals openly states that a metal roof isn't for everyone, even though it's the only product they sell. This kind of transparency is counterintuitively trust-building because so few companies are willing to say it.

key_questions.question: How is this different from a regular FAQ page?
key_questions.answer: A FAQ page answers operational questions. Problems content goes deeper, addressing the emotional concerns buyers have about whether a purchase is the right decision. It reads less like documentation and more like an honest conversation about the real risks involved.

key_questions.question: How do we find the right problems to write about?
key_questions.answer: Start with your sales team. Every objection they hear regularly is a problem worth addressing in content. Review your one-star reviews, customer complaints, and common support questions. These are the exact concerns buyers are researching before they reach out.

title: Versus and Comparisons Content
article_body:
Every buyer compares. It is not a habit of difficult customers or indecisive buyers — it is how informed decisions get made. Before anyone signs a contract, makes a purchase, or books a call, they are stacking you against something else. Maybe it is a named competitor. Maybe it is the option of doing nothing. Maybe it is a different solution category entirely. Whatever the comparison is, it is happening whether or not you are part of the conversation.

The question is not whether your buyers are comparing. The question is whether you are the one helping them do it.

## Why Most Companies Avoid Comparison Content

The most common objection is that comparison content will send buyers to competitors. It won't. Buyers are already looking at competitors. They search "[your product] vs [competitor]" before they ever call you. If you are not the one who answers that search, a competitor's website will, a review site will, or a Reddit thread will — and you will have no say in how the comparison gets framed.

The second objection is bias. "How can we write a comparison that isn't just promotional?" The answer is honesty. Comparison content that acknowledges when a competitor is genuinely better for a specific situation builds more trust than content that pretends you win every comparison. Buyers can detect self-serving spin immediately. Honest comparison content reads differently — and that difference is what earns the trust that leads to a sale.

## What Comparison Content Looks Like

Comparison content falls into several types. Direct competitor comparisons answer searches like "[Your Company] vs [Competitor]." These are among the highest-intent searches a buyer can make — they are already close to a decision. Category comparisons address questions like "fiberglass vs concrete vs vinyl pools" or "HubSpot vs Salesforce vs Pipedrive." These help buyers understand which type of solution is right for them, not just which specific vendor.

There are also approach comparisons — questions like "should I hire in-house or outsource?" or "is it better to build or buy?" These do not compare vendors directly, but they address the fundamental question a buyer is asking about how to solve their problem. Companies that provide honest, thorough answers to these questions position themselves as trusted advisors rather than vendors.

## The Law of the Coin in Comparisons

The Law of the Coin says that every purchase decision has two sides: reasons to buy and reasons not to buy. Buyers will research both. Comparison content that only addresses the positive side of your offering is just marketing copy with a "vs" in the title. It doesn't hold up, and buyers know it.

Effective comparison content shows both sides of every coin. When a competitor is genuinely better at something, say so — and then explain the situations where your solution is the stronger fit. This approach requires confidence, but it consistently outperforms promotional comparisons on trust, search performance, and conversion.

## How to Write Comparison Content That Ranks and Converts

Start with the exact search query your buyer is typing. Title your content to match it — "[Option A] vs [Option B]: Which Is Right for You?" Explain who each option is best for. Acknowledge the strengths of the alternative. Be clear about where your solution wins and where it might not be the best fit. End with a clear recommendation that helps buyers make a confident decision.

The companies that commit to honest comparison content consistently find that it becomes some of their highest-converting content on the site. Buyers who arrive via a comparison search are close to a decision. When your content gives them what they need to decide confidently, many of them decide in your favor.
excerpt: Buyers compare their options before making any significant purchase. The companies that lead that comparison conversation on their own website earn trust and win business. The ones that ignore it lose buyers to whoever is willing to be honest.
what_youll_learn: Buyers compare their options before making any significant purchase. They search for versus and comparison content regardless of whether you publish it.
Comparison content that acknowledges when a competitor is genuinely better in some situations builds more trust than content that claims you win every comparison.
The three main types of comparison content are direct competitor comparisons, category comparisons, and approach comparisons — each serves a different stage of the buyer's research.
The Law of the Coin applies: buyers are researching both sides of every decision, and honest content that covers both sides consistently outperforms promotional content.
Comparison content attracts buyers who are close to a decision — making it one of the highest-converting content types when done honestly.

key_questions.question: Won't comparison content send buyers to my competitors?
key_questions.answer: Buyers are already looking at your competitors before they call you. If you don't address the comparison, someone else will — on a review site, a competitor's blog, or a Reddit thread you have no control over. Addressing it yourself puts you in the role of trusted advisor rather than one of the options being judged.

key_questions.question: How do I write a comparison without it being obviously biased?
key_questions.answer: Be genuinely honest about the situations where a competitor or alternative is the better fit. Most buyers can detect spin immediately. Comparison content that acknowledges real trade-offs reads as credible. Content that pretends you win every comparison reads as marketing copy and gets dismissed.

key_questions.question: Should I name specific competitors?
key_questions.answer: Yes, when buyers are explicitly searching for that comparison. If buyers search "[your product] vs [competitor]" and you don't have a page for it, you're handing that conversation to whoever does. Name the competitor, be fair about their strengths, and be clear about where you differ.

key_questions.question: What if a competitor is genuinely better than us in some ways?
key_questions.answer: Say so. Acknowledging a competitor's real strengths — while being clear about where you are the stronger fit — is one of the most trust-building things a company can do. Buyers respect honesty. It signals that everything else you say is trustworthy too.

title: Reviews Content
article_body:
Rarely do we make a significant purchase without reading reviews first. Whether the platform is Amazon, Google, Yelp, or Reddit, buyers want to know what real customers experienced before they commit. And when they read reviews, they're not looking at the five-star entries. They're going straight to the one-star complaints, the criticisms, the accounts of what went wrong. That's where they find the truth they need to make a decision.

Despite knowing how important reviews are, most companies take a passive approach. They wait for reviews to arrive rather than asking for them. They leave their reputation entirely in the hands of third-party sites. And when they do create review content themselves, they only show the positives, which means the content comes across as promotional rather than trustworthy.

## Why Reviews Matter More Than Ever

In an AI-driven search environment, reviews are not just a buyer's tool — they're a signal that AI systems use to evaluate and recommend businesses. AI models factor in platforms like Google Reviews when determining which businesses to surface in a response. A company with a thin review profile or unaddressed negative reviews is less likely to be recommended by AI than one with an active, honest review presence.

This means generating and managing reviews is no longer optional. It's a core part of how you build trust in the marketplace, both with buyers who read them and with the AI systems that increasingly mediate those buyers' search journeys.

## Getting More Reviews Intentionally

Asking for reviews needs to become part of every delivery process. Ask every customer, every time, immediately after the experience is complete. Don't wait — the moment someone is most enthusiastic about working with you is the moment right after you've delivered something valuable. That enthusiasm fades quickly.

Where possible, automate the follow-up. Triggered emails or text messages sent immediately after a purchase or project completion can dramatically increase review volume. Include a direct link to your Google Business profile or preferred review platform. Remove every possible point of friction between the customer's positive experience and their published review.

Small incentives can help — a discount on a future purchase, a token of appreciation — as long as you're not pushing people toward only positive reviews. What you want is honest feedback at scale, not manufactured five-star ratings. Buyers can tell the difference, and so can AI.

Respond to every review, including the negative ones. This is one of the most overlooked trust-building opportunities available. A sincere, non-defensive response to a critical review signals to every future buyer who reads it that you take problems seriously and care about your customers' experiences. Handled well, a negative review followed by a thoughtful response can be more trust-building than a string of unaddressed five-star ratings.

## Creating Your Own Review Content

Beyond managing third-party reviews, companies that sell products should also create their own review content — articles, videos, or audio recordings that honestly review what they sell. The instinct of many businesses is to leave this to Amazon, YouTube influencers, or editorial sites. But that means leaving the conversation about your own products in someone else's hands.

Self-created review content works because it follows the Law of the Coin. A review that covers both who the product is a good fit for and who it is not carries far more credibility than a marketing page that only talks about the benefits. Buyers expect marketing to be promotional. A review that acknowledges limitations is a surprise — and that surprise creates trust.

## BTOD.com: Review Content as a Business Model

Greg Knighton started BTOD.com (Beyond the Office Door) as an office furniture ecommerce company at a time when the space was crowded and competitive. His path to differentiation was total commitment to reviews: honest, thorough, creative, and relentless.

His homepage prominently displays more than 3,200 Trustpilot reviews with a 4.8 TrustScore. Every product on his site shows a review score. His YouTube channel, BTODtv, has produced dozens of review videos with titles like "We Picked the Best Office Chair for EVERY Price," "I Tested 1-Star Office Chairs," and "I Picked the Most Comfortable Office Chair for the Lowest Price." The videos have generated millions of views and turned BTOD.com into one of the most recognized names in the office furniture space.

One comment on the BTODtv channel captures what happens when a company commits to honest reviews: "Checked out all your reviews with the Herman Miller and Steelcase chairs. Out of all of them, the Mirra 2 was the most adjustable and it ticked all the boxes for me. Ended up buying the fully loaded Mirra 2. My butt and back thanks your in-depth reviews!"

That's what reviews content at its best looks like: a buyer using your content to make a confident decision, and then crediting your honesty for the outcome. That's the business you're building when you take reviews seriously.
excerpt: Reviews shape buying decisions more than almost any other factor. Businesses that take an intentional approach to generating, showcasing, and creating their own reviews consistently build stronger trust.
what_youll_learn: Reviews are one of the primary signals AI models use when recommending businesses. A weak review profile hurts your visibility in AI-driven search.
Most companies make three mistakes with reviews: no intentional plan to generate them, no original review content, and review content that only shows the positive.
Ask for reviews consistently and immediately after delivering value — don't wait. Strike while the experience is fresh.
When creating your own product or service reviews, always apply the Law of the Coin: state clearly who it is a good fit for and who it is not.
Responding to negative reviews publicly builds more trust than a string of unaddressed five-star ratings because it shows how you handle problems.
BTOD.com built a category-defining brand in office furniture almost entirely through a deep commitment to honest review content and testimonials.

key_questions.question: Should we create review content about our own products and services?
key_questions.answer: Yes. Leaving your reputation solely in the hands of third-party sites is a risk. Create your own review content, apply the Law of the Coin honestly, and distribute it across your website, YouTube, email, and social media.

key_questions.question: What is the Law of the Coin in the context of reviews?
key_questions.answer: It means showing both sides of the purchase: who the product or service is a good fit for, and who it is not. Reviews that only celebrate the product feel promotional. Reviews that acknowledge real limitations feel trustworthy.

key_questions.question: How do we get more customer reviews without bribing people?
key_questions.answer: Ask every customer, immediately after delivery. Automate follow-up requests by email or text. Make it easy with a direct link. Respond to all existing reviews, including negative ones. The more friction you remove, the more reviews you'll get.

key_questions.question: How should we respond to negative reviews?
key_questions.answer: Thoughtfully and publicly. Potential buyers pay close attention to how businesses respond when something goes wrong. A sincere, non-defensive response to a critical review often builds more trust than a batch of perfect five-star ratings.

key_questions.question: Do reviews matter for AI-driven search?
key_questions.answer: Yes, significantly. AI models factor in review signals from platforms like Google Reviews when determining whether to recommend a business. A thin or poor review profile reduces your likelihood of appearing in AI recommendations.

title: Best in Class Content
article_body:
When buyers are in research mode, one of the most common things they do is search for the best option available. Best plumber near me. Top-rated project management software. Most reliable HVAC brand. Best CRM for small businesses. This behavior is universal, and it's not going away. Buyers use superlatives to orient themselves in a landscape of options, and the brands that show up for those searches are the ones that lead the conversation.

Most companies avoid this category of content for the same reason they avoid comparison content: they don't want to name competitors, and they worry about appearing self-promotional. So they stay quiet. And every day, buyers search for "best [what they sell]" and find content produced by someone else — a media outlet, a review site, or a competitor willing to participate.

## The Scope of Best-in-Class Searches

The word "best" is just the most obvious trigger. Buyers use a wide range of superlatives when researching options: most reliable, highest rated, lowest maintenance, fastest to install, safest, longest-lasting, cheapest without sacrificing quality. Any of these patterns can anchor a piece of content that captures buyers at exactly the right moment in their research process.

Yale Appliance, featured in the introduction to this methodology, built a massive content library around exactly these searches. Their article and video series on the least serviced, most reliable appliance brands attracted buyers who were doing exactly this kind of research — trying to find the right answer before making a significant purchase. That content positioned Yale as the most knowledgeable source in their market.

## The Million-Dollar Article That Named Competitors

Marcus Sheridan had just lost a sales appointment to a couple in Richmond, Virginia who wanted to see a few more pool companies before deciding. On the drive home, he realized they had essentially asked him: "Who are the best pool builders in Richmond?" So he went home and wrote exactly that article.

He listed five pool builders in Richmond. He chose them because they were the companies he'd lost the most deals to over the years. He didn't include his own company on the list, deliberately avoiding any appearance of bias. His partners thought he had lost his mind.

The result: the article has since generated more than $1 million in revenue for his company. It ranked not just for "best pool builders in Richmond" but also for several of the competitors' keywords. One customer told him directly: "I was about to sign with one of the companies on your list. I stumbled across your article. I thought, 'These guys are so honest, I should call them too.' Then I bought a pool from you."

The insight is simple: buyers are going to find a best-of list one way or another. If you're the company that publishes it — honestly, with real evaluations — you become the most trusted voice in the conversation, even if your own company isn't at the top of the list.

## Best-in-Class Content and AI Recommendations

AI models are increasingly drawing on best-of lists and ranking content when generating recommendations for users. When someone asks an AI assistant "What's the best option for X?" the AI needs sources to draw from. Companies with a strong library of honest best-in-class content are better positioned to be cited by those systems.

This introduces a balance to navigate. You want your content to be useful to AI as a source of genuine recommendations, which means it needs to be honest rather than self-promotional. A best-of list that evaluates the real landscape of options will be treated as a credible source. A list that's obviously designed to promote your own company will not.

## How to Start with Best-in-Class Content

Begin with the superlative questions your buyers are already asking. Your sales team will know these: "Who's the best [type of company] in [city]?" or "What's the best [product category] for [specific need]?" These are often the questions prospects ask at the end of a sales call, right before they say they want to look at a few more options.

Build content that genuinely answers those questions. Give real evaluations. Name options. Explain what makes each one appropriate for different buyers and situations. Use your expertise to provide context buyers can't easily find elsewhere.

Done well, best-in-class content captures buyers at the highest point of their research intensity — the moment they're actively trying to figure out who to trust. That's exactly the moment you want to be the voice they find.
excerpt: Buyers search for the best, the top, the most trusted. Companies that lead those conversations — honestly and openly — capture search traffic, AI visibility, and buyer trust that competitors miss entirely.
what_youll_learn: Buyers instinctively search for the best, highest-rated, most reliable, or top-performing option. This behavior is universal.
Most companies avoid best-in-class content because they fear it will expose them to competitive comparisons. The ones who lean in are the ones who dominate the conversation.
You don't always have to include yourself in a best-of list to benefit. Being the company that educates buyers on the landscape builds authority regardless.
Marcus Sheridan wrote an article on the best pool builders in Richmond without including his own company, and it generated more than $1 million in revenue.
AI models increasingly draw on best-of lists and rankings when making recommendations, which gives this content category growing strategic importance.
The key to best-in-class content is honesty. Self-serving lists that lack genuine evaluation will not build trust and may actively undermine it.

key_questions.question: Should we include our own company in best-of lists we publish?
key_questions.answer: Use judgment. Marcus Sheridan originally left his own company off best-of lists to avoid appearing biased, and it worked extremely well. As AI increasingly draws on these lists for recommendations, there may be cases where including yourself with honest context is appropriate. The test is whether your inclusion serves the buyer's understanding or just your promotion.

key_questions.question: What if we're not actually the best option in every category?
key_questions.answer: Good best-in-class content doesn't require you to win every comparison. It requires you to be honest about what each option is best for. If a competitor's product is genuinely better for a specific use case, say so. That honesty is what makes the content credible.

key_questions.question: What kinds of best-in-class content should we start with?
key_questions.answer: Start with the questions your sales team hears most: 'Who are the best [type of company] in [location]?' and 'What is the best [product type] for [specific need]?' These are the searches buyers are already running, and most companies won't touch them.

key_questions.question: Does best-in-class content work for service businesses?
key_questions.answer: Yes. In fact, service businesses often find it especially effective because most competitors refuse to participate. A law firm, accounting practice, or consulting firm that creates honest comparative content about top options in their category stands out dramatically.

key_questions.question: How does this content perform with AI search?
key_questions.answer: Very well. AI models are increasingly trained to draw on comparative and ranking content when users ask for recommendations. A strong library of best-in-class content makes your site a more authoritative source for AI to cite.

title: The Perfect Pricing Page
article_body:
One of the most effective tools IMPACT has developed for helping companies build trust online is a format they call the Perfect Pricing Page. It's based on a simple insight: buyers don't need an exact number to feel informed. They need to understand the full cost landscape of a purchase, including what drives prices up, what drives them down, and where different options fall on the spectrum. When you provide that, trust follows.

The Perfect Pricing Page isn't a rate card or a quote generator. It's a structured educational resource designed to answer the pricing questions buyers always have but most companies never address. Done well, it's the single piece of content most likely to generate qualified leads and shorten your sales cycle.

## The Five Core Elements

The most important part of a pricing page is covering the five questions every buyer has about cost. These five elements are the foundation. Everything else is supporting content.

What drives costs up in your industry? Help buyers understand what they're actually paying for when prices are higher. This might be quality of materials, level of customization, specialized expertise, longer project timelines, or the scope of service included. When buyers understand what pushes price up, higher-priced options feel less arbitrary.

What drives costs down? Are there ways to get a more affordable version of what you sell? What does a buyer sacrifice in exchange for a lower price? This is especially valuable for buyers who are price-sensitive — it helps them make an informed tradeoff rather than defaulting to the cheapest option without understanding what that choice means.

Why are some companies more expensive? Don't leave buyers guessing about premium pricing. Explain what typically justifies higher prices in your industry: premium materials, more experienced teams, longer warranties, more comprehensive service, or a track record of results. Buyers who understand the reasons behind higher prices can evaluate whether those reasons matter to them.

Why are some companies cheaper? If competitors undercut you and you stay silent about why, buyers assume you're the one overcharging. Explain what lower prices typically reflect in your industry: overseas production, thinner service, less experienced personnel, shorter warranties, or cut corners in delivery. Buyers often choose the cheapest option by default not because they're price-motivated, but because no one educated them about what that choice actually means.

Where does your pricing generally fall? Be direct about where you sit in the market and why. If you deliberately chose a certain price point because of the quality you deliver, say so. Help buyers understand the relationship between what they pay and what they get.

## Supporting Elements That Strengthen the Page

Once the five core questions are answered, additional elements can make the page even more useful for buyers doing serious research.

Pricing tiers work well for many industries. Framing options as low-end, mid-tier, and high-end gives buyers a concrete framework for understanding the range. It also positions your company within that framework, so buyers can see where you fit and why.

Financing and lifetime cost are worth addressing for any significant purchase. A buyer focused only on initial cost may not realize that a higher upfront investment is actually cheaper over five years, or that financing makes a premium option more accessible than it appears.

Visual examples with price ranges add concreteness. Charts, graphics, or side-by-side comparisons help buyers calibrate their expectations without the page needing to commit to a specific quote.

A pricing FAQ section addresses the follow-on questions buyers typically have after reading the main content. Common questions include whether financing is available, what payment terms look like, whether prices vary by location, and whether there are package options.

## Pairing Written and Video Content

The Perfect Pricing Page works as a written article, as a video, or as both combined on the same page. Many companies find the best results come from a written article that covers the full content, paired with an embedded video that walks through the same material conversationally. The written version serves search intent and thorough researchers. The video serves buyers who prefer watching over reading and creates a more personal connection.

When prospects arrive at a sales conversation having already watched your pricing video and read your pricing article, the early stages of that conversation look completely different. They're not asking "how much does this cost?" — they already know the range and understand the value. They're asking whether you're the right fit. That's exactly where the conversation should begin.
excerpt: A great pricing page doesn't require you to publish a fixed number. It requires you to educate buyers on the full cost landscape of your industry, helping them understand value before they ever talk to sales.
what_youll_learn: The Perfect Pricing Page isn't a price list. It's a structured educational resource that helps buyers understand the full cost landscape of your industry.
The five most essential elements are: what drives costs up, what drives them down, why some companies charge more, why some charge less, and where your pricing generally falls.
Pricing tiers (low, mid, high) give buyers a framework for comparing options intelligently, without requiring you to name a specific price.
Financing, lifetime cost versus initial cost, and visual examples are all supporting elements that strengthen a pricing page.
This format works equally well as a written article, a video, or both. Many companies get the best results by pairing the two.
A well-built pricing page shortens sales cycles because prospects arrive already informed about cost, value, and what to expect.

key_questions.question: Do we have to name an exact price on the pricing page?
key_questions.answer: No. The goal is to educate buyers on the range of cost and what drives it, not to publish a rate card. Marcus Sheridan's article about fiberglass pool costs never named a specific price and still generated more than $35 million in revenue.

key_questions.question: What is the most important element to include?
key_questions.answer: The five core elements: what drives costs up, what drives them down, why some companies are expensive, why some are cheap, and where your pricing generally falls. If you cover those five well, the page will do its job.

key_questions.question: Should we create one pricing page or multiple?
key_questions.answer: If you sell multiple distinct products or services at significantly different price points, a separate page for each is worth considering. Otherwise, a single comprehensive page that addresses the full range is usually sufficient.

key_questions.question: How long should a pricing page be?
key_questions.answer: Long enough to genuinely educate. Most effective pricing pages run 1,500 to 3,000 words for a written article. The goal is thoroughness, not length for its own sake. If a buyer finishes reading and still has major unanswered questions about cost, the page hasn't done its job.

key_questions.question: Should we include a video on our pricing page?
key_questions.answer: Yes, when possible. A video that walks through the same pricing content as the article significantly increases engagement and trust. Many buyers prefer watching over reading, and the combination of both formats reaches more of your audience.

title: Video Strategy
article_body:
Video is the closest thing businesses have to a conversation at scale. When someone watches a video of a subject matter expert explaining how something works, walking through a comparison, or sharing what a customer experienced, they're not just gathering information — they're forming a relationship. They're deciding whether they trust you before they ever reach out.

Most companies underuse video entirely, or they produce video without a strategy. They create a brand overview once, post it on their homepage, and consider the job done. That's not a video strategy. A video strategy means creating the right types of videos, optimizing them for the right platforms, and deploying them at the right moments in the sales and marketing process.

## The Two Video Frameworks

The Endless Customers approach to video is built around two complementary frameworks. The Selling 7 covers the seven types of videos that most directly support the sales process: cost and price videos, the 80% video, product and service fit videos, landing page videos, customer journey videos, bio videos, and claims we make videos. These are the videos that shorten sales cycles, build individual trust, and move prospects from consideration to commitment.

The Big 5 applied to video extends the same content topics that drive trust in written articles — cost, problems, comparisons, reviews, and best-in-class — into video format for YouTube and social. These videos drive discovery. They reach buyers who are in the research phase and haven't yet found you, building awareness and trust at scale.

## Long-Form and Short-Form Serve Different Goals

Long-form video (typically five to twenty minutes) is where depth lives. YouTube is the home for long-form video content. These videos educate buyers thoroughly, answer complex questions, and build the kind of trust that comes from someone spending real time with your thinking. Long-form is especially effective for existing audiences who want to go deeper.

Short-form video (typically 5 to 90 seconds) is where awareness lives. YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, TikTok, and Facebook Reels are the platforms. Short-form reaches new audiences, expands brand visibility, and works as a top-of-funnel discovery tool. The average person watches over an hour of short-form video per day. If your buyers are in that population — and they almost certainly are — short-form is a channel you can't ignore.

The smartest approach is to plan content that can live in both formats. A 15-minute YouTube video on the cost of your service generates five to ten short-form clips that can run across social for weeks. Your long-form content investment multiplies when you build a repurposing workflow from the start.

## YouTube as a Core Channel

YouTube is the second-largest search engine in the world and one of the most effective paths to appearing in Google search results. Studies suggest YouTube videos are fifty times more likely to appear in Google results than written content. For companies trying to be found by buyers who are actively researching, YouTube is a search channel as much as it is a social one.

Your YouTube channel should be treated with the same level of care as your website: consistent branding, organized playlists, optimized titles and descriptions, and a regular publishing cadence. A channel that hasn't been updated in six months doesn't inspire trust. One that publishes consistently, answers real buyer questions, and features the actual people buyers will work with is one of the most powerful trust assets a business can build.

## The Investment Required

Executing a serious video strategy requires people, equipment, and consistency. For most Endless Customers companies, this means hiring a full-time in-house videographer. The role covers production, editing, distribution, and the ongoing creation of new content across all formats. A skilled videographer working inside your business, surrounded by your subject matter experts, can produce a volume and quality of content that no outsourced agency or part-time arrangement can match.

Companies that commit to this investment consistently see shorter sales cycles, higher close rates, and dramatically stronger brand recognition. The ones that treat video as a nice-to-have remain dependent on cold outreach, trade shows, and referrals to fill their pipeline. The gap between those two outcomes is one dedicated video hire and a clear content plan.
excerpt: Video is the most powerful trust-building medium available to businesses today. Understanding how to use it strategically — for search, for sales, and for social — is a core requirement of the Endless Customers methodology.
what_youll_learn: Video is now the most effective trust-building medium online. Businesses that avoid it are leaving significant trust and revenue on the table.
There are two primary video frameworks in Endless Customers: The Selling 7 for sales-driven content and The Big 5 applied to video for marketing reach.
YouTube is the second-largest search engine in the world. Treating it like an afterthought means missing one of the most valuable discovery channels available.
Short-form vertical video (YouTube Shorts, Reels, TikToks) is where attention is concentrated today. It works differently from long-form and requires its own strategy.
Structure matters as much as content. Videos without a clear hook, flow, and payoff lose viewers quickly regardless of topic quality.
Most companies produce too few videos, use the wrong types, and deploy them in the wrong places. Getting this right is one of the highest-leverage activities in the Endless Customers system.

key_questions.question: How much video production quality is required?
key_questions.answer: Your videos don't need to be Hollywood productions, but they do need to be clear, well-lit, and audible. Poor audio is the most common reason viewers stop watching. You don't need expensive equipment, but a proper microphone and decent lighting are non-negotiable.

key_questions.question: Who should be on camera?
key_questions.answer: Your salespeople, subject matter experts, and company leaders. The people your buyers will eventually work with. Bio videos, sales support videos, and educational content are most effective when delivered by the people who actually know the subject. Video creates a relationship before the first meeting.

key_questions.question: Where should our videos live?
key_questions.answer: On YouTube as a primary home, embedded on your website's relevant pages, and distributed through short-form clips on social media. Every long-form video can generate multiple short-form clips for Reels, Shorts, and TikTok.

key_questions.question: How often should we publish videos?
key_questions.answer: Consistency matters more than frequency. One well-made video per week, published consistently, will outperform a burst of videos followed by silence. Commit to a cadence you can sustain.

key_questions.question: Does video content apply to B2B companies?
key_questions.answer: Yes, and in many cases B2B companies benefit more because their competitors are less likely to be doing video well. B2B buyers research purchases extensively, and video gives them a way to evaluate your team, your thinking, and your approach before they ever have a conversation.

title: Big Five in Video
article_body:
When Marcus Sheridan wrote his original They Ask, You Answer, the focus was primarily on written content. But as the methodology evolved into Endless Customers, one thing became clear: the five content topics that build the most trust in written articles work just as powerfully — and in many ways more powerfully — in video format.

Buyers researching cost, comparing options, or trying to understand potential problems with a product will watch a video from a credible expert just as readily as they'll read an article. In many cases, they prefer the video, because seeing and hearing a real person address a question carries a different kind of trust than text on a page. The face, the tone, the willingness to speak on camera about a difficult topic — these signals communicate honesty in a way that written content can't fully replicate.

## Applying Each of The Big 5 to Video

Cost and price videos address what buyers pay for your product or service, what drives cost up and down, and why pricing varies across the industry. A well-made cost video is often the first piece of content a serious buyer will watch, because pricing is top of mind before almost any other consideration. Many businesses have written pricing articles; almost none have made an honest pricing video. That gap is an opportunity.

Problems videos address the concerns and fears buyers have about a purchase. Sheffield Metals' "7 Common Problems of a Metal Roof" video generated more than half a million YouTube views because it addressed something buyers were actively researching and couldn't find anywhere else in their industry. The combination of their article and video became a dominant trust signal for the brand.

Comparison videos stack your product against alternatives, or compare different approaches within your category. These work especially well on YouTube because comparison searches are some of the most common buying-related queries on the platform. Buyers typing "X vs. Y" into YouTube are in an active decision-making phase, and a well-made honest comparison video positions you as the most trusted voice in the room.

Review videos cover both third-party social proof and honest first-person evaluations of products or services. BTOD.com's YouTube channel is one of the clearest examples of what a commitment to video reviews can do — millions of views, a category-leading brand, and customers who cite specific videos as the reason they chose to buy.

Best-in-class videos address ranking and superlative questions: what's the best option for a specific need, which brand is most reliable, what the top-rated solutions are in a category. These videos perform exceptionally well in search because they match exactly how buyers phrase their questions when they're trying to make a final decision.

## YouTube as the Primary Platform

YouTube is the right home for Big 5 video content. It is the world's second-largest search engine, and Google's algorithms prioritize YouTube videos in their own results — giving your video content a significant advantage over written articles for many buying-related queries. Publishing on YouTube and then embedding the video on your website's relevant pages is the most effective approach.

A well-made Big 5 video on YouTube can generate qualified traffic and leads for years after it's published. Unlike paid advertising, which stops the moment you stop paying, a strong organic video continues to compound in value over time. Leading companies treat their YouTube libraries as long-term assets, not one-off campaigns.

## Repurposing for Short-Form Distribution

Every long-form Big 5 video generates raw material for multiple short-form clips. A twelve-minute pricing video might contain five to eight moments that can be extracted and reformatted as sixty-second vertical videos for YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, and TikTok. This repurposing workflow dramatically extends the reach of each video investment and reaches buyers who are actively consuming short-form content on social platforms.
excerpt: The same five content topics that drive trust in written articles perform just as powerfully in video. Applying The Big 5 to your YouTube and social video strategy builds awareness and trust at a scale written content alone cannot reach.
what_youll_learn: The Big 5 topics — cost, problems, comparisons, reviews, and best-in-class — perform as well in video as in written articles, often better.
Video adds a dimension of trust that written content can't replicate: buyers see and hear a real person, which accelerates confidence in ways text alone cannot.
YouTube is the primary home for Big 5 video content. These videos also generate clips for short-form social distribution.
Most companies won't make a video discussing their pricing, their product's problems, or a competitor comparison. The few that do dominate those searches.
A single Big 5 video often performs for years after it's published, generating qualified traffic and leads continuously.
Leading companies integrate Big 5 content across all video platforms, not just their website, multiplying reach and trust signals.

key_questions.question: Which Big 5 topic performs best in video format?
key_questions.answer: All five perform well, but cost and price videos and comparison videos tend to generate the most search volume. Problems content and reviews content generate strong engagement because they address the emotional concerns buyers have. Best-in-class content performs especially well in video because it often has a visual or demonstration component.

key_questions.question: How long should Big 5 videos be?
key_questions.answer: Long enough to genuinely answer the question. Most cost and comparison videos run five to twelve minutes. Problems videos might be shorter or longer depending on how many issues you're covering. Quality and completeness matter more than hitting a specific runtime.

key_questions.question: Should Big 5 videos go on YouTube or just our website?
key_questions.answer: YouTube should be the primary publishing platform. Then embed each video on the relevant page of your website. This approach maximizes reach through YouTube's search engine while also strengthening the trust and depth of your website pages.

key_questions.question: Can we create Big 5 videos without professional production equipment?
key_questions.answer: Yes. Clear audio, decent lighting, and a real person speaking credibly about the topic are the requirements. Many of the most effective Big 5 videos are simple talking-head videos recorded in an office. The content and honesty of what's said matters far more than production quality.

key_questions.question: Should we create short-form clips from our Big 5 videos?
key_questions.answer: Absolutely. Every long-form Big 5 video can generate five to ten short-form clips for YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, and TikTok. This multiplies the reach of each video investment significantly.

title: YouTube Strategy for Endless Customers
article_body:
YouTube is the second-largest search engine in the world, and it isn't close to being a social media platform in any meaningful sense. People go to YouTube with questions, intent, and purchasing decisions in mind. More than 70% of people use it to evaluate products and services or solve problems they're experiencing at work or in their lives. That number is growing. For companies implementing Endless Customers, YouTube is not optional.

The urgency matters even more now that AI platforms are reshaping how people find information. As tools like ChatGPT and Perplexity reduce the number of Google searches that result in a website click, companies that relied entirely on traditional SEO are watching their traffic decline. YouTube provides a powerful counter to that trend. Google prioritizes YouTube videos in its search results — roughly 80% of video results on Google come from YouTube — and videos appear at a dramatically higher rate than text pages for searches related to buying decisions.

## Treat YouTube Like Your Website

The companies that succeed on YouTube are the ones that treat their channel with the same strategic discipline as their website. That means organized playlists for key topics, consistent branding, descriptive titles and tags that match what buyers are actually searching for, and a regular publishing schedule. A YouTube channel with ten videos and no updates in eight months signals neglect, not authority.

Every video you publish on YouTube becomes a permanent, searchable asset. A well-produced video on 'what does a roof replacement cost in [your city]' can drive traffic and leads for years after you publish it. Your YouTube channel is not a campaign — it is a library. Treat it that way.

## What to Publish

The content that performs best on YouTube for Endless Customers businesses is the same content that performs best everywhere else: Big 5 topics and Selling 7 videos. Cost and price videos, comparison content, best-in-class guides, problem-solution videos, and customer journey stories are all topics buyers are actively searching for on YouTube. Because you're answering real questions rather than producing promotional content, these videos earn genuine viewer trust.

Aim for at least two new videos per week. Each video should address a specific buyer question, not a broad topic. 'Everything About Our Industry' is not a YouTube video. 'How Much Does a Custom Pool Cost in Phoenix?' is.

## Episodic Content and Repurposing

One of the highest-leverage approaches on YouTube is episodic content: structured video series that follow a predictable format, cover a consistent topic area, and give viewers a reason to come back. A series built around customer journey stories, or a weekly Q&A series answering the most common questions in your industry, builds the kind of audience loyalty that compounds over time.

Episodic content also solves the repurposing problem. Each long-form YouTube video can generate short-form clips for social media, audio for a podcast feed, written transcripts for your blog, and highlights for your email newsletter. A single production session becomes multiple pieces of content across multiple channels. This is what it looks like to think like a media company.

## YouTube and Sales

YouTube is not only a marketing tool. Your sales team should be actively sharing YouTube videos with prospects through Assignment Selling, directing them to relevant content before discovery calls. When a prospect watches your Cost and Price Video on YouTube before speaking with a salesperson, the tone of that conversation changes entirely. They arrive informed rather than guarded, which shortens the sales cycle and improves close rates.

Your YouTube channel is one of the most powerful trust-building assets your business can build. Unlike paid ads that disappear when the budget stops, a well-produced YouTube library grows in value over time. Start publishing consistently, stay focused on buyer questions, and treat the channel as the permanent, searchable asset it is.

key_questions.question: Why does YouTube matter so much for Endless Customers businesses?
key_questions.answer: Because buyers use YouTube to research purchases, evaluate vendors, and learn about categories before they ever contact a company. If you're not on YouTube answering the questions your buyers are already asking there, a competitor will be. YouTube is also increasingly important as AI tools and zero-click search reduce traditional Google traffic — companies that build strong YouTube channels have a visibility channel that doesn't depend on search clicks.

key_questions.question: How is YouTube different from other social media platforms?
key_questions.answer: YouTube behaves more like a search engine than a social platform. People go to YouTube with specific questions and intent, searching for tutorials, product information, comparisons, and reviews. That intent-driven behavior makes YouTube viewers more qualified and more likely to take action than passive scrollers on other platforms. A video published on YouTube can drive traffic for years — unlike a social post that disappears in days.

key_questions.question: How often should we publish on YouTube?
key_questions.answer: At minimum, aim for two new videos per week. Consistency matters more than volume. A dead channel signals a dead company. Algorithms reward regular publishing, and so do subscribers who come to expect new content on a regular schedule. Build a backlog before you launch so you never miss a week.

key_questions.question: What types of videos should go on our YouTube channel?
key_questions.answer: Big 5 content and Selling 7 videos form the core. Cost and price videos, comparison and review content, problem-solution videos, product and service fit videos, and customer journey stories all perform well on YouTube. These are the exact topics your buyers are already searching for — which is why this approach consistently produces measurable results.

key_questions.question: Do we need a professional production setup for YouTube?
key_questions.answer: No. Your videos need to be clear, engaging, and professional — but they do not need to be Hollywood productions. Good audio matters more than expensive cameras. A genuine, knowledgeable person on camera matters more than high-end graphics. Companies that obsess over production values while avoiding the camera consistently underperform companies that get on camera regularly with genuine content.

title: Short-Form Video
article_body:
Short-form vertical video has fundamentally changed how people consume content online. YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, TikTok, and Facebook Reels collectively capture more daily viewing time than almost any other category of media. The average person watches more than an hour of short-form video per day — a number that continues to grow.

Many business owners and marketing leaders resist short-form video because they don't personally consume it, or because it feels like a consumer entertainment platform rather than a business tool. This is a mistake rooted in personal preference rather than buyer behavior. The buyers researching your products and services are in this audience. Meeting them on platforms they already use is simply smart business.

## What Short-Form Video Is For

Short-form video is primarily an awareness tool. It reaches buyers who don't yet know you exist. When someone scrolling through Reels encounters a video that addresses a question they have — whether it's a quick tip, an honest comparison, or a moment from a longer expert conversation — they experience your brand for the first time in a way that feels natural rather than intrusive.

Long-form video builds depth with people who already know you. Short-form builds width — it expands the number of people who know your brand exists and have a positive first impression of it. Both are necessary, and they serve different goals.

## Bringing The Big 5 to Short-Form

Short-form video is an effective distribution channel for Big 5 content topics. A quick take on what drives cost up in your industry, a direct answer to a common buyer concern, a rapid-fire comparison of two options — these topics work in sixty seconds just as they work in ten minutes. The format is different, but the principle is the same: answer the questions buyers are already asking, honestly and on camera.

Comparison content performs especially well in short-form because viewers enjoy the format and find it useful. A thirty-second video that shows a clear side-by-side comparison of two options can stop a scroll and earn a follow from someone who was moments ago completely unfamiliar with your brand.

## The Repurposing Workflow

The most efficient path to a strong short-form presence is to build repurposing into your long-form production process. Every YouTube video, every recorded webinar, every expert interview contains moments that can be extracted, reframed vertically, and published as short-form clips. A single hour of long-form production can yield a month of short-form content with the right workflow.

This approach has a secondary benefit: short-form clips can drive viewers back to the long-form source. Someone who watches a sixty-second clip and wants to go deeper has a clear path to the full video. Short and long form are not competing strategies. They work together.

## What Makes Short-Form Perform

The algorithm on every short-form platform rewards two things above all else: click-through rate and retention rate. Your hook determines whether someone watches. Your structure determines whether they finish. High retention signals quality to the platform, which responds by showing the video to more people.

The guiding principle for short-form structure is: make them click, make them stick. Get to the point immediately. Remove every moment that doesn't advance the story or the value. End the video the instant the payoff is delivered. These are not suggestions — they are the structural requirements for short-form video that actually distributes. The Sticky 5 framework covers the specific mechanics in detail.
