Short-form content performs best when it is fast, focused, and ends decisively. The Quit While You're Ahead Principle is critical.
Content that works well on one short-form platform generally translates to others. Plan for cross-platform distribution from the start.
Every long-form video you produce should generate multiple short-form clips. This repurposing workflow multiplies your investment.
Businesses that dismiss short-form video because they don't personally consume it are making decisions based on personal preference rather than buyer behavior.

key_questions.question: Should B2B companies be doing short-form video?
key_questions.answer: Yes. The buyers at B2B companies are the same people watching Reels and Shorts in their personal time. Meeting them on platforms they already use builds recognition and trust that carries over into professional decisions. B2B companies that are early to short-form in their category often develop significant awareness advantages.

key_questions.question: How do we come up with enough content for short-form?
key_questions.answer: Start with your long-form library. Every Big 5 video, Selling 7 video, or educational video you produce contains multiple moments that work as short-form clips. A twelve-minute YouTube video might yield six to eight Shorts. Build short-form into your production workflow rather than treating it as a separate effort.

key_questions.question: What makes short-form video perform well algorithmically?
key_questions.answer: Click-through rate and retention rate are the primary signals. Your hook (the first second or two) determines whether someone watches. The structure of your video determines whether they finish. High retention tells the algorithm the content is good, which leads to wider distribution.

key_questions.question: How often should we publish short-form content?
key_questions.answer: More frequently than long-form. Most companies aiming for YouTube Shorts or Reels target three to five posts per week. Consistency matters more than volume. Start with what you can sustain and build from there.

key_questions.question: Do short-form videos need professional production quality?
key_questions.answer: No, and over-producing them can hurt performance. Short-form audiences respond well to authentic, natural-feeling content. Good audio and decent lighting are the only technical requirements. Everything else is secondary to the quality of the hook and the value of the content.

title: The Sticky 5
article_body:
Short-form video lives and dies by one metric: how long viewers watch. Platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram measure retention rate as one of their primary quality signals. A video that holds viewers until the end gets shown to more people. A video that loses viewers in the first few seconds gets buried. The Sticky 5 is a framework built entirely around retention.

The guiding phrase is simple: make them click, make them stick. Getting someone to tap on your video is only the first challenge. Keeping them through to the payoff is the real measure of whether the video will perform.

## The Five Principles

The Hook is the title and the first one to two seconds of the video. This is where you establish a curiosity gap — something that makes the viewer feel they'll miss something important if they keep scrolling. The best hooks are specific, unexpected, or directly address a concern or question the viewer already has. The hook must relate to what the viewer actually sees in that first frame. If the visual doesn't match the hook, viewers feel deceived and leave.

The 3-Second Rule is about maintaining visual momentum. Ideally, there should be a cut, angle change, or new visual element every three seconds. This keeps the video feeling like it's always moving. Watching a static shot for ten seconds in a short-form video feels like an eternity. Constant visual variety signals that something interesting is always about to happen.

The Progress Principle means every moment should contribute to a feeling of forward movement. The viewer should feel, moment by moment, that the video is getting somewhere. Any scene, shot, or statement that doesn't clearly advance the story or the point should be cut. Lulls hurt retention more than any other structural problem.

The Payoff Principle is about delivering a genuine reward at the end. Every viewer who watches a short-form video is implicitly asking "Was this worth my time?" The payoff is your answer. It should feel satisfying, complete, and proportionate to the expectation set by the hook. Strong payoffs tend to generate emotional responses — surprise, satisfaction, delight, or even mild shock — and those emotional responses translate into shares and comments.

The Quit While You're Ahead Principle may be the most counterintuitive of the five. The second the payoff is delivered, the video should end. No summary, no call to action, no waving goodbye. Cut immediately. Even two or three seconds of footage after the peak moment will cause retention rates to drop — and that drop signals to the algorithm that the video lost the viewer's interest, which reduces distribution.

## What Happens When You Get It Right

Short-form videos with strong retention rates can achieve what's called a "loop" — where the ending flows naturally back to the beginning, causing viewers to watch again without realizing it. Retention rates above 100% are possible, meaning the average viewer watches the video more than once. This is the signal every platform algorithm is looking for when deciding which videos to push to wider audiences.

Marcus Sheridan's fishing channel, Saltwater Fishing University, offers a clear example. When capturing a large fish, the video ends the instant the fish lands in the boat. The crew celebration afterward is cut entirely, even though it's satisfying to film. The payoff is the catch. Once it's there, the video is over. That discipline is what drives strong retention and, in turn, wider reach for every video the channel publishes.
excerpt: The Sticky 5 is a five-part framework for structuring short-form video to maximize retention, boost algorithmic reach, and build the kind of viewer engagement that turns views into followers and followers into buyers.
what_youll_learn: Short-form video performance is measured primarily by retention rate. The Sticky 5 is built to maximize it.
The Hook must be established in the first one to two seconds. If the opening doesn't create curiosity or intrigue immediately, most viewers will scroll past.
The 3-Second Rule means keeping cuts, angle changes, or new visuals coming constantly. Things should feel like they're always moving.
The Progress Principle means every moment should feel like it's getting somewhere. Remove anything that doesn't contribute to forward movement.
The Payoff Principle is about delivering a genuine emotional or informational reward at the end. The ending should feel satisfying and complete.
The Quit While You're Ahead Principle says to end the video the instant the payoff is delivered. Even two seconds of unnecessary footage after the peak will hurt retention.

key_questions.question: Why does retention rate matter so much?
key_questions.answer: Retention rate is one of the primary signals short-form platforms use to decide how widely to distribute a video. A video where most viewers watch until the end gets shown to more people. A video where most viewers drop off early gets buried. The Sticky 5 is designed to maximize how long each viewer stays.

key_questions.question: What makes a good hook for a short-form video?
key_questions.answer: A hook creates a curiosity gap — it makes the viewer feel like they'll miss something important if they keep scrolling. The best hooks are specific, unexpected, or directly address a question or concern the viewer already has. Vague or generic openings don't stop scrolls.

key_questions.question: How short is short enough for the Quit While You're Ahead Principle?
key_questions.answer: The video should end the moment the payoff is complete. Not after a call to action, not after a summary, not after the presenter waves goodbye. The second the main point or moment has landed, cut. Some of the best-performing short-form videos end so abruptly that the viewer watches again just to confirm they saw it right — which pushes retention above 100%.

key_questions.question: Does The Sticky 5 apply to all short-form platforms?
key_questions.answer: Yes. The underlying principles of retention, momentum, and a decisive ending apply across YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, TikTok, and Facebook Reels. The tactical specifics (ideal length, aspect ratio) vary slightly by platform, but the Sticky 5 framework applies universally.

key_questions.question: Can we apply The Sticky 5 to repurposed long-form clips?
key_questions.answer: Yes, and this is one of the most common applications. When extracting clips from a longer video, choose moments that already have a natural hook, build toward a clear payoff, and end cleanly. Trim aggressively before and after to preserve the structure.

title: The Selling 7
article_body:
For more than a decade, IMPACT has been helping businesses use video strategically to support the sales process. In that time, a clear pattern emerged: certain types of videos consistently moved the sales needle, while others had little measurable impact. The seven that reliably drove results became known as The Selling 7.

These are not brand awareness videos or product highlight reels. The Selling 7 are strategic assets designed to address specific moments in the buyer's journey, answer the questions buyers most commonly have, and build personal trust before the first conversation happens. Companies that create all seven and deploy them intentionally see measurable differences in sales cycle length, close rates, and the quality of prospects who reach the sales team.

## The Seven Types

The 80% Video answers the questions your sales team gets asked on nearly every call. When a prospect watches this video before a sales conversation, the call starts in a fundamentally different place. Operational questions are already answered. Both sides can focus on whether there's a genuine fit.

Bio videos introduce individual salespeople in a personal and approachable way. Buyers want to know who they're going to work with. A salesperson who sends a bio video before the first meeting arrives at that meeting as a familiar face rather than a stranger. That small shift changes the entire dynamic of the conversation.

Product and service fit videos live on product pages and answer the question "Is this right for me?" They follow the Law of the Coin — honest about who the product is and is not a good fit for — which makes them far more credible than promotional demos.

Landing page videos sit next to forms on contact or conversion pages and tell visitors exactly what will happen after they submit. They address the four questions almost every buyer has before filling out a form: Will you spam me? Will you call me repeatedly? What happens to my information? What comes next? Adding this video to a landing page typically increases form conversions by up to 80%.

Cost and price videos bring the transparency of The Big 5 pricing content into video format. A salesperson or subject matter expert on camera discussing what drives cost up, what drives it down, and where your pricing generally falls creates a level of trust that a written article alone often cannot.

Customer journey videos tell the story of a real customer's experience: the problem they faced, the journey they went on with your company, and the transformation that resulted. These videos are the most powerful form of social proof available because they let buyers see themselves in a customer who was once exactly where they are now.

Claims we make videos prove the things your company says about itself. Every company claims to have great service, dedicated teams, and outstanding results. Most never prove it. A video that demonstrates — with evidence, with customer voices, with real examples — why a claim is true is far more credible than the claim stated in an ad.

## Where to Start

For companies new to The Selling 7, the fastest wins come from bio videos for the sales team and the 80% Video for each major product or service. These two types directly improve active sales conversations and can be created relatively quickly.

Customer journey videos and cost and price videos are the next priority, followed by landing page videos and claims videos. Most companies that commit to The Selling 7 over a 12-month period find that building out the full library keeps one in-house videographer busy throughout the year — and that the investment pays for itself quickly in closed revenue.
excerpt: The Selling 7 are seven specific types of videos proven to shorten sales cycles, increase close rates, and build buyer trust before the first conversation. Every sales-driven organization should have all seven.
what_youll_learn: The Selling 7 are not marketing videos — they are strategic tools designed to move buyers from research to decision.
The 80% Video alone can transform a sales team's efficiency by answering the most common questions prospects have before the first call.
Bio videos create personal trust before a single conversation happens. A prospect who has watched a salesperson's bio video already feels like they know them.
Landing page videos have been shown to increase form conversion rates by up to 80%, nearly doubling the number of leads generated from existing traffic.
Customer journey videos are the most powerful form of social proof available because they tell the full story — the problem, the journey, and the transformation.
Most companies create none of The Selling 7. Companies that create all seven have a measurable sales advantage that compounds over time.

key_questions.question: How long do Selling 7 videos need to be?
key_questions.answer: It depends on the type. Cost and price videos typically run five to eight minutes. The 80% Video is often similar in length. Bio videos are short — one to three minutes. Landing page videos should be under two minutes. Customer journey videos are usually three to five minutes. Claims videos vary based on what's being proven.

key_questions.question: Who should appear in each type of video?
key_questions.answer: Cost, problems, and comparison videos work best with subject matter experts. Bio videos should feature each individual salesperson. Customer journey videos star your customers. Claims videos can feature team members, customers, or a combination. The key is that real people appear on camera — not animated graphics or voiceovers.

key_questions.question: Should we start with all seven at once or prioritize?
key_questions.answer: If resources are limited, start with the 80% Video and bio videos for your sales team — these have the most immediate impact on active sales conversations. Cost and price videos and customer journey videos come next. Landing page and claims videos can follow.

key_questions.question: Where do Selling 7 videos live?
key_questions.answer: Primarily on your website, embedded on the relevant pages — product pages, contact pages, team pages. The 80% Video and bio videos are shared directly by salespeople via email and in proposals. Customer journey videos also belong on social media and YouTube.

key_questions.question: How do we measure whether these videos are working?
key_questions.answer: Track close rates before and after implementation, sales cycle length, and the number of prospects who arrive at a sales call already familiar with your pricing and team. Also track form conversion rates when you add landing page videos. Most companies see measurable changes within 90 days.

title: The 80% Video
article_body:
Ask any experienced salesperson what percentage of the questions they get on sales calls are essentially the same, regardless of who's on the other end. The answer is almost always between 70 and 90%. Prospects ask the same questions about how your process works, what your pricing looks like, how long things take, what the common concerns are, and what differentiates you from competitors. Every single call.

The 80% Video is built on a simple premise: if you already know what those questions are, answer them before the call happens. Put a real person on camera, walk through the most common questions prospects have, and send that video to every prospect before their first meeting with your team.

## What Changes When Prospects Watch First

A prospect who arrives at a sales call having already watched the 80% Video is a fundamentally different kind of conversation partner. They've processed the foundational information. They've already decided whether the basic parameters work for them. The conversation can start at a level of specificity that typically takes multiple calls to reach without the video.

This benefits both sides. The prospect isn't wasting time on questions they'll find answered in the video. The salesperson isn't spending the first third of every call on the same educational overview. Both sides can get to the real conversation faster: is this a fit, and what would it look like to work together?

## How to Build the 80% Video

Start by gathering your sales team for a brainstorm. The goal is a list of the questions that come up on virtually every call. Include the questions about price, process, timeline, common concerns, how you compare to alternatives, and what makes you different. These are your topics.

Then put a subject matter expert or senior salesperson on camera and have them walk through those questions conversationally. The format is simple: address each question directly, honestly, and with the same tone and depth they'd bring to a live conversation. There's no need for elaborate production. A clean background, good audio, and a natural delivery are all you need.

Create a separate 80% Video for each major product or service. The questions a prospect has about one offering are likely different from those they'd have about another. Each video should be specific enough to be genuinely useful rather than a generic company overview.

## How to Deploy It

The 80% Video should live on the relevant product or service page of your website. But the most powerful use is proactive: salespeople send it to prospects as part of their meeting confirmation. A simple note that says "before we talk, here's a video that covers the questions most people have" prepares the prospect and signals that your company values their time.

The 80% Video is one of the highest-leverage tools in the Selling 7. It pays for itself in the first few sales cycles it improves, and its compounding value — better-prepared prospects, shorter cycles, higher close rates — grows over time as more buyers engage with it before they ever speak with your team.
excerpt: 80% of the questions your sales team answers on every call are the same. The 80% Video answers those questions before the call happens — transforming your sales conversations and saving everyone's time.
what_youll_learn: Sales teams across virtually every industry report that 70 to 90% of the questions they answer on calls are essentially the same.
The 80% Video answers those questions before the first sales conversation, so the call can start at a higher level of trust and specificity.
Every major product or service you offer should have its own 80% Video.
When a prospect watches the 80% Video before a sales call, both sides benefit: the prospect is better informed, and the salesperson can skip educational basics and get to the real conversation.
The 80% Video should be sent proactively by salespeople before meetings, not just published on a website.
The name comes from the observation that roughly 80% of sales questions are universal — the remaining 20% are where real sales skill is applied.

key_questions.question: How do we know which questions to include?
key_questions.answer: Ask your sales team. Sit in on calls. Review recorded sales conversations. The questions that come up on nearly every call are your 80%. Most sales teams can identify them in a 30-minute brainstorm.

key_questions.question: How long should the 80% Video be?
key_questions.answer: As long as necessary to answer the core questions thoroughly. Most run five to ten minutes. Quality and completeness matter more than keeping it short. A prospect who leaves the video still having major unanswered questions will bring those to the call anyway.

key_questions.question: Should the 80% Video be on our website?
key_questions.answer: Yes, ideally on the relevant product or service page. But the most impactful use is having salespeople send it directly to prospects before scheduled meetings, with a note like 'this video covers the questions most people have before we talk.'

key_questions.question: Do we need a separate 80% Video for each product?
key_questions.answer: Yes, if your products or services are meaningfully different. The questions prospects have about product A are likely different from the questions they have about product B. Each deserves its own video.

key_questions.question: What happens to sales call dynamics when prospects watch the 80% Video first?
key_questions.answer: The call starts at a much higher level. Prospects have already processed the foundational information and often arrive with more specific, focused questions. Close rates tend to improve because buyers are better qualified before the conversation begins.

title: Bio Videos
article_body:
One of the most powerful things video does for a business is let buyers meet your people before they ever pick up the phone or fill out a form. Buyers don't just evaluate products and services — they evaluate the people they'll be working with. Bio videos give them a way to do that on their own terms, at their own pace, before any commitment is made.

A salesperson who sends a bio video before the first meeting arrives at that meeting as a familiar face. The awkward early moments of two strangers getting acquainted are largely gone. The buyer has already formed a positive initial impression. The conversation starts from a place of warmth rather than wariness.

## What to Include

A strong bio video covers two things. First, what you do and why you love it. This is the professional context: the role, the experience, the types of clients or problems you most enjoy working on. It gives the buyer a sense of your competence and commitment.

Second, something personal. Where you grew up, your family, a hobby you're serious about, something that makes you a real person rather than a job title. Buyers don't need to know your life story, but they need to see that there's a person behind the role. This is what creates the feeling of familiarity that makes the first conversation feel less like a sales call and more like catching up with someone they've already met.

## Where Bio Videos Belong

The most impactful home for a bio video is the salesperson's email signature. Every email they send to a prospect includes a link or thumbnail to their bio video. Prospects can watch before any meeting, and many will. Some will watch multiple times. By the time the first call happens, they feel prepared in a way they normally wouldn't.

Bio videos also belong on your team page and on any booking or scheduling page where prospects confirm a meeting. If someone is scheduling time with a specific salesperson, showing them that person's bio video on the confirmation page is a simple way to set a warmer tone before the conversation begins.

## Getting Your Team to Do It

Many salespeople resist being on camera, especially for something as personal as a bio video. The best way to handle this is to lower the bar. Remind them that authenticity is the point. A slightly imperfect, natural delivery is more appealing than a scripted, rehearsed performance. Shoot in a comfortable setting, let them speak naturally, and don't over-produce the result.

The salespeople who start using bio videos almost universally report that the dynamic of their first meetings improves. Prospects mention the video. Conversations start warmer. Close rates trend upward. The feedback loop tends to eliminate any remaining resistance quickly.
excerpt: People buy from people they trust. Bio videos let buyers meet your salespeople before the first conversation, turning strangers into familiar faces and reducing the friction of the first meeting.
what_youll_learn: Buyers are more likely to show up to a meeting and more comfortable in the conversation when they've already seen the person they'll be talking to.
Bio videos should be personal, not polished. Authenticity matters more than production quality.
Every salesperson should have a bio video embedded in their email signature.
The two key elements are: what they do and why they love it, and something personal about who they are.
A prospect who has watched a salesperson's bio video arrives at the call feeling like they already know them. That feeling is the foundation of trust.
Bio videos are one of the fastest Selling 7 videos to produce and one of the highest-impact for immediate sales conversations.

key_questions.question: How long should a bio video be?
key_questions.answer: One to three minutes is the target. Long enough to feel genuine and personal, short enough that a prospect will actually watch it. Cover the two core elements — professional background and personal connection — without padding.

key_questions.question: Where should bio videos live?
key_questions.answer: In each salesperson's email signature is the most impactful placement. The bio video link goes out with every email, so every prospect has the opportunity to watch before their first call. Bio videos should also live on the team or about page of your website.

key_questions.question: What should salespeople say in their bio video?
key_questions.answer: Cover what they do and why they love it, then add something personal — family, hobbies, where they grew up, something that makes them a real person rather than a job title. The goal is for a prospect to finish watching and feel like they already know this person a little.

key_questions.question: Does production quality matter for bio videos?
key_questions.answer: Less than for other video types. A clean background, good audio, and natural delivery matter more than professional camera work or editing. Overly produced bio videos can feel less personal, which defeats the purpose.

key_questions.question: Should non-sales team members also have bio videos?
key_questions.answer: Yes, for anyone who works with clients directly. Project managers, account managers, customer success teams — anyone a buyer will eventually work with benefits from having a bio video. The earlier a buyer can see the people they'll be working with, the more comfortable they feel moving forward.

title: Product and Service Videos
article_body:
Every product and service page on your website is an opportunity to answer the question buyers always have when they land there: is this right for me? A well-written page can go a long way toward answering that question. A video answers it better — faster, more personally, and in a way that text alone rarely achieves.

The problem with most product and service videos is that they're pitch videos. They cover features, benefits, and positive outcomes. They don't address who the product is not right for. And because buyers know that promotional content is designed to be one-sided, those videos don't build the trust they're intended to build.

## The Law of the Coin in Product Videos

A product and service fit video applies the Law of the Coin directly: it covers both sides. Who is this a genuinely good fit for? What kind of buyer, situation, or use case does it serve well? And equally important: who is it not a good fit for? What buyer or situation would be better served by a different option?

When a video says something like "this is not the right choice if you need X" — and means it — something shifts in the viewer's perception. They recognize that the person on camera is trying to help them make a good decision, not just close a sale. That recognition is the beginning of real trust.

## What to Cover

A strong product or service fit video typically covers: what the product or service is and who it's designed for, what problem it solves and for whom, who it works especially well for, who it's not a good fit for and why, what buyers typically experience or achieve when they use it, and what the next step is if it does seem like a fit.

Keep the video under five minutes for most products and services. Buyers visiting a product page want to make a decision efficiently. Give them what they need to determine fit, and point them to the next step. The goal is clarity, not comprehensiveness.

## What Changes When These Videos Are Present

Pages with honest fit videos tend to see higher engagement, longer time on page, and better conversion rates. When buyers can see and hear a real person walk through whether the product is right for them, the self-selection process improves. The people who reach out after watching tend to be better-matched to what you offer, which makes sales conversations more productive and close rates stronger.
excerpt: Every product and service page on your website should have a video that helps buyers answer one question: is this right for me? Following the Law of the Coin makes these videos far more credible than typical promotional demos.
what_youll_learn: Product and service videos should answer the question 'Is this right for me?' not just 'What does this do?'
Following the Law of the Coin means covering both who the product is a good fit for and who it is not.
Most product videos are pitch videos that only show the positive side. That's not what buyers trust.
These videos belong on every product and service page on your website.
Keep product and service videos under five minutes when possible. Buyers need clarity, not a comprehensive tour.
A video that honestly addresses fit — including situations where your product might not be the right choice — is far more trusted than one that only promotes benefits.

key_questions.question: Should we use these videos to actively sell or to inform?
key_questions.answer: To inform, primarily. The goal is to help buyers self-qualify. When the video honestly addresses fit — including who shouldn't buy — buyers who proceed to reach out are already better matched to what you offer. This makes the sales conversation more efficient and close rates higher.

key_questions.question: What happens if we say the product isn't right for some buyers?
key_questions.answer: Buyers trust you more. Saying 'this is not a good fit for X type of customer' signals that you have the buyer's best interest in mind, not just making a sale. The Law of the Coin requires both sides, and the businesses that apply it build significantly stronger brand trust.

key_questions.question: How long should these videos be?
key_questions.answer: Under five minutes is the target for most product or service fit videos. Buyers visiting a product page want clarity quickly. Cover the key fit questions, show what it looks like, address the good fit and bad fit scenarios, and stop.

key_questions.question: Should the video be scripted or natural?
key_questions.answer: A general outline works better than a word-for-word script. Scripted videos often feel stiff and rehearsed, which reduces trust. Conversational delivery, with natural pauses and real language, tends to land better with buyers evaluating whether they trust your team.

key_questions.question: Can we use screenshots, demos, or walkthroughs in these videos?
key_questions.answer: Yes, especially for software and digital products. Showing the product in action alongside a person explaining the fit criteria makes the video more concrete and useful. Just keep the demo grounded in 'here's who this is for' rather than 'here's everything the product can do.'

title: Landing Page Videos
article_body:
When a visitor lands on a form page and considers filling it out, four concerns almost always arise. Will this company spam me if I give them my email? Will they call me repeatedly? What will they do with my personal information? And what exactly happens next if I submit?

These concerns are the primary reason qualified visitors abandon forms. They're interested enough to have read the page. They're interested enough to consider reaching out. But they're not sure what they're agreeing to, and they'd rather leave than find out the hard way.

A landing page video answers all four concerns in under two minutes. The result, consistently across IMPACT's client base, is a conversion lift in the range of 80% — nearly double the number of people who fill out the form.

## What the Video Says

The most effective landing page videos open by naming the concerns directly. Something like: "You might be sitting there wondering if we're going to spam your inbox or call you every day. Here's exactly what's going to happen after you fill out this form." Then walk through the process step by step. Then address what won't happen: no spam, no harassment, no sharing your information with third parties.

The video can also explain the timeline (when will they hear back and how), what the first conversation looks like, and what the visitor should expect as the next step. Every element is designed to reduce uncertainty, because uncertainty is the primary driver of form abandonment.

## Why This Works

The reason landing page videos are so effective is the same reason all the content in the Selling 7 is effective: they treat the buyer like an intelligent adult who has reasonable concerns, and they address those concerns directly before being asked. The visitor realizes that this company is willing to be transparent about the process, which changes their perception of the risk involved in reaching out.

This video is also one of the fastest to produce. One person on camera, one to two minutes of honest, conversational explanation, minimal editing required. The return on the time invested is among the highest of any video type in the Selling 7.

## Where to Apply It

The most immediate application is any high-intent conversion page: contact us, request a consultation, get a quote, book a call. These are the pages where a motivated buyer is making a decision to reach out. The landing page video reduces the final barrier between their interest and their action.
excerpt: Adding a short video to a form page that explains exactly what happens after submission has been shown to increase conversion rates by up to 80%. It's one of the simplest, highest-return videos a business can make.
what_youll_learn: Most visitors who abandon a form do so because of four unresolved concerns: spam, repeated calls, data privacy, and uncertainty about what comes next.
A landing page video that addresses all four concerns before submission has consistently produced conversion lift of up to 80%.
The video should be short — under two minutes — and conversational in tone.
The script should open by naming the concerns directly: 'You might be wondering if you'll get spammed...'
This is one of the fastest videos to produce and one of the highest-return investments in the Selling 7.
Landing page videos work on contact pages, consultation request forms, quote request pages, and any other high-intent conversion page.

key_questions.question: What exactly should the video say?
key_questions.answer: Address the four concerns directly. Example script: 'You might be wondering if we're going to spam you or call you ten times a day. Here's exactly what will happen after you fill out this form: [explain the process]. Here's what won't happen: [address spam and excessive calls]. Your information stays private and is only used to [specific purpose].' Be direct, be honest, be brief.

key_questions.question: How long should the landing page video be?
key_questions.answer: Under two minutes. The goal is to remove anxiety and answer a short set of specific questions. A longer video will be ignored by the same visitors you're trying to convert.

key_questions.question: Who should appear in the video?
key_questions.answer: Ideally, the person the visitor will actually hear from after they submit. If leads go to a specific salesperson or coordinator, that person introduces themselves in the video. This pre-establishes the relationship and reduces friction even further.

key_questions.question: Where exactly should the video be placed on the page?
key_questions.answer: Next to the form, at the same level. The visitor should be able to see both the video and the form at the same time. A title like 'See exactly what happens when you fill out this form' with a thumbnail that shows a real person works well.

key_questions.question: Will this video hurt conversion rates if visitors watch it and decide not to submit?
key_questions.answer: In practice, the opposite happens. Visitors who were going to convert convert more confidently. Visitors who weren't going to convert weren't going to convert anyway. The net effect on qualified lead volume is positive.

title: Cost and Price Videos
article_body:
The Cost and Price Video is the first of The Selling 7, and it belongs first because pricing is almost always the first real question a prospect has. You may have already addressed cost in written content — a blog post, a pricing page, or an FAQ. The Cost and Price Video takes that same transparency and brings it to life on camera, where tone, explanation, and personality can do things a written page cannot.

The strategic value of this video is simple: a salesperson can share it with a prospect before a discovery call. Instead of walking into that call cold — with pricing uncertainty already creating friction — the prospect arrives having watched your rep or a company leader explain cost honestly, in their own words, to every decision-maker involved in the purchase. No secondhand summaries. No misquoted numbers. Just a clear, direct explanation they can pause, rewatch, and share internally.

## What Belongs in the Video

A well-made Cost and Price Video covers three things. First, it addresses the factors that influence what your product or service costs — materials, labor, scope, customization, geography, or whatever actually drives the number in your business. Second, it puts your pricing in market context, explaining why similar products or services can vary widely in price and what separates a cheaper option from a more expensive one. Third, it makes the case for your own pricing — not defensively, but clearly, explaining what buyers get for what they pay.

The goal is not to close the sale in the video. The goal is to eliminate the anxious, half-formed question about cost that sits in every prospect's mind and replace it with a clear, honest answer. Buyers who feel they understand your pricing before a call are buyers who arrive with their guard down. They're ready to talk about fit rather than fencing over numbers.

## One Video Per Product or Service

If your company offers multiple main products or services, create a separate Cost and Price Video for each one. A single video that tries to cover everything becomes too vague to be useful. A prospect evaluating your enterprise software package and a prospect evaluating your entry-level plan have different questions, and each deserves a direct answer. Specificity is what makes these videos effective in an actual sales conversation.

## How Long Should It Be?

Most Cost and Price Videos run five to eight minutes. That is long enough to be genuinely thorough and short enough to hold the attention of a motivated buyer who actually wants to understand what they're about to spend. Do not pad the video to hit a target length, and do not cut it short to seem concise. Follow the content. If your offering is straightforward, five minutes may be plenty. If it involves significant complexity, customization, or comparison with competitors, take the time the topic requires.

## Production and Delivery

These videos do not need to be over-produced. A clear image, good audio, and a genuine on-camera presence from someone the prospect will actually meet are more valuable than high-end graphics. What prospects want is to feel like they're getting a real conversation with someone honest, not a polished pitch from a company trying to hide something.

Once created, these videos are deployed through Assignment Selling — shared by a salesperson in a one-to-one video message or email before a scheduled call. They also belong on relevant product and service pages on your website, where prospects doing their own research can find them. The same transparency that builds trust in a sales conversation builds trust in organic search.

The Cost and Price Video is one of the highest-leverage investments a company can make in its video strategy. It directly addresses the single most common reason a sales conversation breaks down before it begins. Make it honest. Make it specific. And put it to work.
excerpt: The most powerful cost and price content you can create isn't a written article — it's a video a salesperson can send directly to a prospect. Here's how to create one that builds trust before the first call.
what_youll_learn: Cost and Price Videos take the transparency of Big 5 pricing content and bring it to life visually, making it easier for prospects to understand value before they speak with anyone.
The video allows your salesperson to communicate cost and value even when they aren't in the room — a recording delivers your message exactly as intended to every decision-maker involved.
Each video should cover the factors that influence price, how your product compares in the marketplace, and why your offering costs what it does.
Create a separate Cost and Price Video for each major product or service you offer — one video trying to cover everything will be too vague to be useful.
These videos typically run five to eight minutes, long enough to be thorough but focused enough to hold attention.
Shared before discovery calls via Assignment Selling, these videos mean prospects arrive informed, which shortens the sales cycle and raises the quality of every conversation.

key_questions.question: Why make a video about cost when I already have a pricing page?
key_questions.answer: A written pricing page and a cost video serve different jobs. The pricing page is found through search. The video is shared by your salesperson directly with a specific prospect before a call. It allows your rep to explain nuance, context, and value in a way that a static page cannot, and it ensures every decision-maker hears the same message in your own words.

key_questions.question: What should a Cost and Price Video actually cover?
key_questions.answer: Three things: the factors that influence the cost of your product or service, how prices vary in your market and why, and why your product costs what it does — your value proposition explained plainly. Avoid vagueness. The goal is to leave no honest question unanswered.

key_questions.question: How long should a Cost and Price Video be?
key_questions.answer: Long enough to be thorough, short enough to stay focused. Most run five to eight minutes. If you have a simple product, it might be shorter. A highly complex offering might need more time. Follow the content, not a target runtime.

key_questions.question: Do I need separate videos for each product or service?
key_questions.answer: Yes. Each major product or service deserves its own video. A single video trying to cover all your offerings becomes too general to help anyone. Specificity is what makes these videos useful in a real sales conversation.

key_questions.question: Who should appear in a Cost and Price Video?
key_questions.answer: Ideally someone the prospect will also speak with — a salesperson, a company leader, or a subject matter expert. The goal is to make the video feel like a direct conversation rather than a corporate production. Authenticity matters more than production polish.

title: Customer Journey Videos
article_body:
Nothing does the trust work of a customer journey video. A prospect who watches a real client describe a challenge they recognize, explain how they found your company and what working with you was like, and then show the results they achieved — that prospect doesn't just feel informed. They feel like they've seen a version of their own story with a good ending.

That recognition is the most powerful conversion tool available. It can't be manufactured with marketing copy or claimed through a list of client logos. It happens when a real person, telling a real story, says something that makes a prospective buyer think: "That's exactly where I am right now."

## The Three-Act Structure

Every customer journey video follows the same arc. Act one is the problem, need, or concern the customer was trying to solve before they found you. What was the situation? What had they tried before? What was the frustration or fear driving them to look for a solution? This is the part that creates connection, because it mirrors what current prospects are feeling.

Act two is the journey. How did they discover your company? What made them decide to reach out? What was the experience of working with your team like? This is where your company appears in the story, but always as the guide rather than the hero. The customer is the hero. You're the company that helped them get where they needed to go.

Act three is the transformation. What changed? What results did they achieve? How is their situation different now than it was before? This is where the payoff lives for the prospect watching, because it shows them where they could be.

## How to Use Them in the Sales Process

Customer journey videos are one of the most effective assets a salesperson can deploy after an initial meeting. After a first conversation, a salesperson can identify which customer journey video most closely mirrors the prospect's situation and send it with a note: "I thought you'd find this relevant given what you shared about your situation." This keeps the relationship warm between meetings and lets a real customer continue the trust-building work that the salesperson started.

On social media, customer journey videos drive the kind of engagement that pure brand content rarely achieves because they tell a real story with real people. Viewers share them. They comment. They tag people they know who are in a similar situation. The video does distribution work that advertising can't replicate.
excerpt: Customer journey videos are the most powerful form of social proof available. They tell the full story — problem, journey, and transformation — and they let prospects see themselves in someone who was once exactly where they are now.
what_youll_learn: Customer journey videos follow a three-act structure: the problem, the journey, and the transformation.
The most powerful moment in these videos is when a past customer describes where they were before. Prospects who see themselves in that description immediately connect.
These videos work across your website, social media, YouTube, and in active sales conversations.
A well-made customer journey video does conversion work that no amount of marketing copy or claimed results can replicate.
Customers who were hesitant at first often make the most compelling subjects because their journey mirrors what current prospects are experiencing.
Unlike testimonials, customer journey videos tell a full story. That narrative arc is what makes them emotionally resonant and trustworthy.

key_questions.question: What's the difference between a testimonial and a customer journey video?
key_questions.answer: A testimonial captures a moment: 'I loved working with this company.' A customer journey video tells a story with three acts: the problem the customer faced, the journey they went through, and the transformation they experienced. The narrative arc is what makes the journey video far more emotionally resonant and useful for prospective buyers.

key_questions.question: Who makes the best subject for a customer journey video?
key_questions.answer: Customers who were skeptical at first or faced real challenges before reaching out often make the most compelling subjects. Their hesitation mirrors what current prospects feel. When they describe overcoming that hesitation and achieving a real result, it gives current prospects a path to follow.

key_questions.question: How long should a customer journey video be?
key_questions.answer: Three to seven minutes works for most. Long enough to tell the full three-act story and let the transformation feel real. Short enough that buyers will watch in full during a sales process or on your website.

key_questions.question: Where should customer journey videos be used?
key_questions.answer: On your website on relevant product or service pages, in active sales conversations (sent by salespeople after an initial meeting), on social media as awareness content, and on YouTube. Salespeople who share a relevant customer journey video after a first call often see significant improvement in follow-through from prospects.

key_questions.question: How do we get customers to participate?
key_questions.answer: Ask the clients you've had the best results with, especially those who were initially hesitant. Most satisfied clients are willing to share their story when asked directly. Make the process easy: a 45-minute recorded conversation is usually enough raw material to produce a strong customer journey video.

title: Claims We Make Videos
article_body:
Every company makes claims. Virtually no company proves them. That gap is exactly what Claims We Make Videos are designed to close.

Think about the statements your sales team makes regularly: our people are what set us apart, our service is exceptional, we stand behind everything we sell. Now think about how many of your competitors say the exact same things. Buyers hear these claims repeatedly, and they have learned to treat them as background noise. A claim without evidence is not a differentiator. It is noise.

Claims We Make Videos are the final type in The Selling 7, and they complete what the other six began: building trust by showing what your competitors aren't willing to show. Where other videos address cost, common questions, and customer journeys, Claims We Make Videos address the specific promises your company makes and provide actual evidence that they're true.

## Start with a Full List of Your Claims

Before making any videos, sit down and list every claim your company makes — in sales conversations, in marketing copy, on your website, and in proposals. You may be surprised how many there are. Common examples include 'our customer service is second to none,' 'our team has more experience than anyone in the market,' 'our guarantee is the best in the industry,' and 'clients who work with us see measurably better results.' Every claim on that list is a video waiting to be made.

Once you have your list, ask a simple question for each claim: How have we proven this is true? If the answer is 'we haven't,' the video makes that proof. If the answer is 'we have customer examples and internal data,' the video captures and presents that evidence clearly.

## Show, Don't State

The distinction between a pitch and a Claims We Make Video is evidence. A pitch repeats the claim with more emphasis. A Claims We Make Video shows something real. If you claim your team is what makes you different, put a team member on camera explaining their specific approach to a problem, walking through how they handled a complex situation, or describing what they do that a competitor wouldn't. The viewer finishes the video knowing more than they knew before — not just hearing the claim again.

If you claim your guarantee is the best, walk through exactly what it covers, what triggers it, and what a customer experiences if they ever need to use it. Read through the actual terms. Show the process. Let a customer who has used it explain what happened. Specificity is credibility. Vagueness is just a claim.

## How These Videos Get Used

Like all Selling 7 videos, Claims We Make Videos are most powerful when deployed by your sales team through Assignment Selling. When a prospect raises a concern or implies skepticism about a specific claim — 'every company says their service is great' — the salesperson can send the relevant video before the next conversation. The prospect watches proof rather than hearing the claim restated.

These videos also belong on your website, near the claims they support. If your About page states that your team is exceptional, a video that proves it belongs on that page. If your guarantee page makes specific promises, the video that walks through those promises belongs there. Every claim on a page is an opportunity to back it up with evidence a visitor can see.

## Why Most Companies Don't Do This

Creating Claims We Make Videos requires something most companies find uncomfortable: honest self-examination. You have to look at each claim and ask whether the evidence actually supports it. If it does, making the video is straightforward. If it doesn't, you either need to stop making the claim or start building the evidence worth showing. Either outcome improves your business.

That discomfort is exactly why most competitors won't do this. They'll continue making the same unsupported claims while their prospects quietly wonder whether any of it is true. Companies willing to put their claims on camera, with real evidence, earn a level of trust that no amount of marketing copy can replicate.

Claims We Make Videos complete The Selling 7. Together, these seven video types cover the most common reasons a sales conversation breaks down — cost uncertainty, unanswered questions, lack of trust, unclear fit, and unproven promises. Address all seven, deploy them through your sales team, and the quality of every sales conversation your company has will rise.
excerpt: Every company claims to have great service, exceptional people, and an industry-leading guarantee. Almost none of them prove it. Claims We Make Videos are how you show buyers the evidence behind every promise you make.
what_youll_learn: Most companies make the same claims — great people, exceptional service, best guarantee — and buyers have learned to ignore them because no one backs them up.
Claims We Make Videos don't state what makes your company different; they show it with real evidence, real examples, and real demonstration.
Start by listing every claim your sales team makes, then ask: how many have we actually proven with video?
Each claim becomes its own video — specific, focused, and demonstrative rather than promotional.
These videos are used the same way as other Selling 7 videos: shared before calls, embedded on relevant pages, deployed through your sales team.
Proving claims on camera is one of the most direct ways to show what your competitors aren't willing to show — because most companies never bother.

key_questions.question: What kinds of claims should these videos address?
key_questions.answer: Any claim your sales team makes repeatedly — especially ones that sound like things every competitor also says. Common examples include: 'our people make us different,' 'our customer service is second to none,' 'we have the best guarantee in the industry.' If you've said it more than once in a sales call and never backed it up with evidence, it belongs on your list.

key_questions.question: How do you actually prove a claim on video?
key_questions.answer: Show the specific thing rather than describe it. If you claim your team is exceptional, put a team member on camera explaining their approach and showing their work. If you claim your guarantee is the best, walk through exactly what it covers and what a customer would experience if they ever needed to use it. Evidence is specific. Promises are vague.

key_questions.question: How many Claims We Make Videos does a company need?
key_questions.answer: Start with a list of every claim your team makes in sales conversations. Each significant claim deserves its own video. Companies with many service promises might need five or ten videos. Companies with a simpler offering might need two or three. The test is whether a prospect watching the video would finish it thinking, 'That claim is actually true,' rather than, 'Okay, that's what they want me to believe.'

key_questions.question: Where do these videos get used?
key_questions.answer: They're most powerful in the sales process, shared by reps as part of Assignment Selling before calls with prospects who have asked or implied a specific concern. They also belong on relevant pages of your website — your About page, your guarantee page, or service-specific pages where the relevant claim is being made.

key_questions.question: Isn't this just a more elaborate marketing pitch?
key_questions.answer: Only if you do it wrong. The distinction between a pitch and a Claims We Make Video is evidence. A pitch says 'we're the best.' A Claims We Make Video shows a real example, a real process, a real customer result, or a real demonstration. If your video ends and a skeptical buyer still has no more reason to believe you than before they watched, you've made a pitch. Start over.

title: Be More Human
article_body:
There is a real risk embedded in the rise of AI: that companies, chasing efficiency, automate away the very thing that made their brand worth trusting. That every email becomes a template. That every piece of content sounds like every other piece of content. That buyers, who already struggle to differentiate vendors, stop being able to distinguish your company from any other company using the same tools.

The antidote is the fourth pillar of a Known and Trusted Brand: Be More Human. Not less. Not the same. More. Use AI to free up time and extend your reach, but invest what you save into showing buyers more of the real people, real stories, and genuine character that make your company worth knowing.

## People Trust People

Look at any industry and compare the personal brand of the company's founder or leader with the brand of the company itself. The person almost always has more attention, more engagement, and more trust. Richard Branson has more pull than the Virgin brand. Gary Vaynerchuk has more pull than VaynerMedia. This pattern holds at every company size. Buyers want to know who they're working with — what they believe, how they think, and whether they can be trusted — before they ever sign anything.

This means the visible people on your sales and marketing team are brand assets. Their ability to be genuine on camera, in writing, and in conversation directly affects how much trust your company earns. A team of recognizable, credible subject matter experts builds a brand that no anonymous company can compete with.

## One-to-One Video in the Sales Process

One of the clearest examples of what it means to be more human in a sales process is one-to-one video. Instead of sending a text email that reads exactly like every other sales email a prospect has ever received, a salesperson records a short personal video — addressing the specific person, their specific situation, and what they specifically discussed or are about to discuss.

The response from prospects is consistently striking. 'I was so impressed that you sent me a video instead of text. No salesperson has ever done that before.' 'I felt like I'd already met you before we even had our first call.' 'Your sales process is more personal and human than anyone else we talked to.' These comments come up again and again, across industries, from teams that adopt this practice.

One-to-one video is cheap, fast, and far more effective at building trust than text. Most sales teams still don't do it. That gap is your opportunity.

## The Authentic 15

Beyond one-to-one video, IMPACT developed a framework called The Authentic 15 — fifteen specific ways to deepen your brand's human connection with buyers over time. These include sharing real employee stories, creating day-in-the-life content, showcasing customer experiences with photos or video, responding genuinely on social media rather than with corporate boilerplate, sharing failures and what you learned from them, using real photos of your actual team and workspace instead of stock images, and giving your leadership a real visible voice rather than a PR-filtered one.

None of these fifteen practices are difficult in isolation. Most companies don't do them consistently because it requires a level of openness and authenticity that feels uncomfortable, especially for leaders who are used to keeping a professional distance. That discomfort is exactly what makes consistency here such a strong competitive advantage. Most competitors won't sustain it.

## Leaders Go First

The most important thing a leader can do is model what it looks like to be human in public. If leadership never sends a personal video, the team won't either. If leadership never shares a story about something that went wrong, the company will feel polished but distant. If leadership is never visible as a genuine person, the brand remains a logo.

The goal is for buyers to feel, before they've ever spoken with anyone on your team, that they already know you. That they've heard your voice, seen your face, and developed a real sense of whether this is a company they want to work with. When that happens consistently, at scale, across your sales and marketing team, you've built the kind of brand that creates endless customers.
excerpt: AI is making content creation cheaper and faster for everyone. The companies that win will be the ones whose content, people, and culture feel unmistakably human. Here's what that looks like in practice.
what_youll_learn: As AI-generated content becomes ubiquitous, human authenticity becomes a stronger competitive differentiator, not a weaker one — buyers increasingly gravitate toward brands with real, visible people behind them.

Personal brands within your company are more important than ever. People trust people more than logos, and buyers are more likely to work with companies whose team members they feel they already know.

One-to-one video in the sales process is one of the most underused and highest-impact ways to humanize your brand — prospects consistently say it makes your team feel more approachable and trustworthy.
Leaders set the tone. If leadership isn't willing to show up on camera, share real stories, or be visible and genuine, the team won't either.
The Authentic 15 is a framework for building a genuinely human brand over time — from sharing real stories and employee spotlights to owning failures and responding authentically on social media.
Humanizing your brand is not a marketing tactic. It is a commitment to showing buyers the real people behind your company, which builds the kind of trust no promotional campaign can replicate.

key_questions.question: Why does being human matter more now that AI can produce content at scale?
key_questions.answer: Because when everyone can generate polished content instantly, the content that stands out is content that feels genuinely human — real stories, real faces, real opinions, real vulnerability. Buyers can tell the difference between a company that uses AI to scale their humanity and one that uses AI to replace it. The companies using AI as a tool to reach more people with their genuine voice will outperform the ones producing generic content at high volume with no real person behind it.

key_questions.question: What is one-to-one video and why does it matter?
key_questions.answer: One-to-one video is a short, personalized video sent by a salesperson directly to a prospect via email or messaging, rather than a generic text email. The salesperson records a brief video addressing the specific person and their specific situation. Prospects regularly respond with comments like 'I was so impressed that you sent a video' and 'I felt like I already knew you before our first call.' The trust it builds is disproportionate to the effort it requires, and most sales teams still aren't doing it.

key_questions.question: What does 'personal brand' mean for someone on a sales or marketing team?
key_questions.answer: It means being a visible, recognizable expert in your field rather than a nameless employee behind a company logo. Personal brand builds when team members publish their thinking, appear on camera, engage authentically on social media, and develop a reputation for genuine expertise. Buyers in every industry increasingly research the specific people they'll be working with before agreeing to a meeting. A team member with a real online presence is far more likely to earn that meeting than one with none.

key_questions.question: What is the Authentic 15?
key_questions.answer: The Authentic 15 is a framework developed at IMPACT that identifies 15 specific ways a company can deepen its human connection with buyers over time. It includes things like sharing real stories from employees and customers, showcasing team members through employee spotlights, responding genuinely on social media, sharing failures alongside wins, creating behind-the-scenes content, and using real photos rather than stock images. These are things most competitors won't do consistently — which is exactly what makes them powerful differentiation.

key_questions.question: How do leaders lead on this?
key_questions.answer: By going first. If the CEO sends one-to-one videos, the sales team will follow. If leadership shares real stories about the company's challenges and lessons learned, the rest of the team will feel permission to do the same. If leaders stay invisible and polished, the entire organization tends to stay invisible and polished. The most human companies are almost always led by people who are themselves willing to be human in public.

title: The Endless Customers Content Team
article_body:
The single most impactful decision a company can make to succeed with Endless Customers is bringing content production in-house. Not delegating it to an agency. Not outsourcing it to freelancers. Owning it internally, with dedicated people whose full-time job is creating and publishing the content your buyers need.

This is a consistent finding across hundreds of companies that have implemented the Endless Customers system. The ones that succeed have in-house teams. The ones that struggle are typically still trying to outsource their way to trust — which almost never works. Outsourced content lacks the expertise, the authentic voice, and the real-world knowledge that makes content worth reading and sharing. Agencies can produce polished material, but they cannot produce the genuine insight that comes from people who actually do the work.

## The Two Core Roles

At the foundation of every Endless Customers content team are two roles: a content manager and a videographer. The content manager owns written content production, SEO, email, distribution, and content strategy. The videographer owns video production, from shooting and editing to coaching team members to perform on camera. Together, these two roles cover the full spectrum of content your buyers consume.

In smaller companies, one person may wear both hats. As a business grows past $5 million in revenue, splitting these into dedicated roles becomes both practical and necessary. At larger companies, the team expands further to include specialists in web management, graphic design, data analysis, and paid media. But the content manager and videographer are the core that everything else builds on.

## Ownership Is Everything

Content production stalls when no one owns it. This is one of the most common implementation failures: a company commits to Endless Customers, everyone is excited about the strategy, and then six months later almost nothing has been published because content has been treated as everyone's responsibility — which means no one's responsibility.

Someone must own the content creation process from start to finish. They publish three or more pieces per week. They interview subject matter experts. They manage the editorial calendar. They review analytics and adjust. They keep the sales team supplied with fresh content to use in the sales process. Without that level of ownership and accountability, the content engine does not run.

## How the Content Team Works with the Rest of the Business

The content team is not an island. Their best content comes from the people inside your business who deal with buyers every day. Sales calls, service delivery conversations, and customer questions are all raw material for content. A good content manager systematically mines those sources, interviewing salespeople and service staff, attending sales calls, and reviewing recordings to capture the real knowledge that buyers want.

The content team also works directly with leadership on the company's messaging and on building the personal brands of the company's visible subject matter experts. Every piece of content published reflects on the company's reputation as the most known and trusted brand in its market. The people responsible for producing that content need direct access, genuine support from leadership, and the freedom to publish honestly rather than through a filter of corporate caution.

## Building the Team Over Time

Start with what you can staff today. For most companies just beginning, that means hiring one strong person who can handle both writing and basic video production while using AI tools to extend their output. Once that person is running and the content engine is producing consistently, the business case for adding a dedicated videographer — or other specialists — becomes clear in the results.

The content team is not a cost center. It is the engine of your market presence. Every article, video, and piece of content it produces is an asset that continues working long after it is published, building the body of trust that converts strangers into buyers and buyers into advocates.
